How to Use This Material
0.1 Who this is for
Someone who has finished the Binary Trees course, or who is comfortable with recursion, vector,
queue, stack, map and basic complexity analysis, and who has never studied graphs.
The target is competitive programming. Everything here is written the way you would actually write
it in a contest: short, fast, 1-indexed, scanf-free but cin-with-fast-IO, global arrays where that is
simpler. Interview style is mentioned where it differs, but contests are the priority .

0.2 What you will be able to do at the end
Read a Codeforces problem, notice that it is a graph problem even when the word “graph” never
appears, build the graph, choose the right algorithm, and implement it correctly the first time.
Concretely, by the end you can solve most graph problems rated up to about 1600, and you will
understand the ideas behind harder ones.
The four questions this course trains you to ask:
What are the vertices, and what are the edges?
Is it directed? Is it weighted? Can it have cycles?
Do I need reachability, distance, ordering, or connectivity?
Which of the eight standard algorithms answers that question?

Part 1
Graph Fundamentals
Vocabulary, and how a graph differs from a tree
1.1 Why graphs exist
A tree can express hierarchy: one parent, many children, no way back up except the way you came.
That is a strong restriction, and most real relationships break it.
• Cities joined by roads. A city has no parent. You can drive in a circle.
• Friendships. If A is a friend of B then B is a friend of A. Not a hierarchy .
• Course prerequisites. Many courses depend on many others, and the dependenc

dships. If A is a friend of B then B is a friend of A. Not a hierarchy .
• Course prerequisites. Many courses depend on many others, and the dependency has a direction.
• Web pages linking to each other. Circular links are normal.
• States of a puzzle, where a move takes you from one state to another.
A graph is the most general “things and connections between them” structure. Trees, linked lists, grids
and hierarchies are all special cases of it. That generality is exactly why graphs are the single largest
topic in competitive programming.
1.2 Definition
A graph is a pair G = (V, E):
• V is a set of vertices, also called nodes. We number them 1 to n.
• E is a set of edges, each edge joining two vertices.
That is the whole definition. There is no root, no parent, no order among the neighbo

1.3 Terminology
Everything below refers to G1.
Vertex (plural vertices): a single item. Also called a node.
Edge: a connection. We write it 1-2 for undirected and 1->2 for directed.
Adjacent: two vertices joined by an edge. 1 and 2 are adjacent. 1 and 3 are not.
Nei

connection. We write it 1-2 for undirected and 1->2 for directed.
Adjacent: two vertices joined by an edge. 1 and 2 are adjacent. 1 and 3 are not.
Neighbour: same thing from one vertex’s point of view. The neighbours of 2 are 1, 3, 4, 5.
Degree of a vertex: how many edges touch it. deg(2) = 4, deg(6) = 1, deg(7) = 1.
Handshake lemma: the sum of all degrees equals 2m, because every edge adds one to the degree of
each of its two endpoints. For G1: 2 + 4 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 16 = 2 * 8. Useful for checking
that you read the input correctly , and for the fact that the total work of visiting all adjacency lists is
O(m), not O(nm).
Walk: any sequence of vertices where consecutive ones are joined by an edge. Repeats allowed.
Path: a walk with no repeated vertex. 1 - 2 - 3 - 6 is a path.

Connected component: a maximal group of mutually connected vertices. G1 has two components:

The single most common bug in beginner graph code is storing an undirected edge only once. An
undirected edge must be pushed into both adjacency lists. Say it out loud every time you write
the input loop.
Directed graphs also complicate connectivity . In a directed graph, “u can reach v” does not imply “v
can reach u”, which is why we need the notion of strongly connected components in Part 13.
1.5 Weighted and unweighted
A weight is a number attached to an edge: length, cost, time, capacity . Unweighted means every edge
counts as 1.

The four practical consequences, and you should write them on the first page of your notebook:
1. Always keep a visited array. Without it, DFS on a cyclic graph never terminates.
2. Always loop over all vertices when you want to cover the whole graph, because one DFS only
covers one component.
3. Complexity is O(n + m), not O(n). You touch every vertex once and every adjacency entry once,
and every undirected edge appears in two lists.
4. Recursion can go n deep. With n = 2 * 105 and heavy stack frames, plain DFS can crash. Keep
the frame small, or write it iteratively .
A tree is not a different data structure from a graph. A tree is a connected undirected graph with
no cycles, equivalently a connected graph with exactly n - 1 edges. Part 12 revisits the whole trees

1.7 Families of graphs worth naming
Tree: connected, acyclic, n - 1 edges, unique path between any two vertices. Adding any edge creates
exactly one cycle, and removing any edge disconnects it.
Forest: a disjoint set of trees. If a graph has c components, no cycles and n vertices, it has exactly n -
c edges.
DAG, directed acyclic graph: directed, no directed cycle. Every DAG has at least one vertex of indegree
0. This is the family where topological sorting and DP on the graph live (Part 8).
Bipartite graph: the vertices split into two sides so that every edge goes betwe

e family where topological sorting and DP on the graph live (Part 8).
Bipartite graph: the vertices split into two sides so that every edge goes between the sides, never
inside one side. Equivalently , no odd cycle (Part 7).
Complete graph K_n: every pair joined. It has n(n-1)/2 edges, which is the maximum for a simple
undirected graph. A directed simple graph maxes out at n(n-1).
Grid graph: an r by c board where each cell is a vertex joined to its 4 (or 8) neighbours. Almost
never given as an edge list, so Part 2 shows the standard trick.
Functional graph: every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge, for example a[i] meaning “i points
to a[i]”. Such a graph is a set of cycles, each with trees hanging off it. Permutations are the special
case where it is exactly a set of cycles.

Implicit or state graph: the vertices are states of some process (a configuration of a puzzle, a position
plus a remaining fuel amount) and the edges are legal moves. You never build the graph, you generate

1.9 Common mistakes
• Adding an undirected edge only once. Half your edges silently vanish.
• Forgetting visited. Infinite recursion, or exponential blowup on graphs with many cycles.
• Running one DFS from vertex 1 and assuming the graph is covered. Only true if the graph is
connected, and the statement must say so.
• Sizing arrays with n instead of n + 1 when vertices are numbered 1 to n.
• Using an adjac

if the graph is
connected, and the statement must say so.
• Sizing arrays with n instead of n + 1 when vertices are numbered 1 to n.
• Using an adjacency matrix when n is 105.
• Assuming there is a path. In a disconnected graph the answer is often “-1”, and problems test
exactly that case.
• Assuming the graph is simple. Self loops and multiple edges break naive cycle detection.
• Assuming a connected graph with n vertices and n - 1 edges is a tree without checking
connectivity. You need both facts, though either one plus acyclicity implies the other.
• Ignoring that m can be 0.

In a binary tree, recursion went as deep as the height, and a balanced tree gave you 20 frames. In a
graph, a sim

ecursion depth, the practical danger
In a binary tree, recursion went as deep as the height, and a balanced tree gave you 20 frames. In a
graph, a simple path
1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - ... - 200000
gives you 200000 nested calls. Each frame holds the parameters, saved registers and the iterator over

code with large local arrays inside the recursive function will not.
Rules that keep you safe:

• Pass few parameters, and pass them by value if they are ints, or by reference if they are containers.
• If the problem has n up to 106, or you are on a judge with a small stack, write the iterative version.

That sentence is the reason BFS matters. Memorise it with its condition: unweighted. The moment

4.2 Why the layers are shortest distances

4.2 Why the layers are shortest distances
BFS processes vertices in non-decreasing order of distance. The argument is short enough to keep in
your head:
• Layer 0 is {s}, at distance 0, obviously correct.
• Suppose every vertex at distance k has been placed in the queue and nothing further has been.
When we pop those vertices and push their unvisited neighbours, any such neighbour must be at
distance exactly k + 1: it cannot be closer, or it would already have been found in an earlier layer,
and it is reachable in k + 1 steps by construction.
So the first time BFS reaches a vertex, it reaches it optimally. That is why we set dist and mark
visited at push time, not at pop time.

9.1 The problem it solves
You have n items, initially all separate. Two operations arrive in any order, many times:
union(a, b) put a and b into the same group
find(a) which group is a in
and the real question is usually find(a) == find(b), meaning “are a and b in the same group”.
DFS answers connectivity once, in O(n + m). It cannot handle edges arriving over time, because
every new edge would need a fresh traversal. DSU handles both operations in essentially constant
time, which is why it appears in an enormous fraction of contest problems.
Other names for it: Union-Find, disjoint set forest.
9.2 The idea
Every group is a tree, and the root of that tree is

find(a); b = find(b);
if (a != b) parent[a] = b;
}
Correct, and potentially O(n) per operation. Union in a bad order builds a chain:
union(1,2), union(2,3), union(3,4), ... produces
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> ... -> n
and find(1) walks the entire chain.
Two independent improvements fix this. Use both.
9.4 Improvement 1: path compression
While walking up in find, point every visited node straight at the root. The next find on any of them
is then one step.
int find(int x) {
if (parent[x] == x) return x;
return parent[x] = find(parent[x]); // compress on the way back up
}
That single line,parent[x] = find(parent[x]), does the whole job. It is a postorder assignment:
recurse to the root first, then rewrite the pointer.

Union by rank (tree height) is an equivalent alternative. Size is more useful, because component sizes
are often part of the answer.

With both improvements, m operations on n elements cost O(m alpha(n)), where alpha is the inverse
Ackermann function. For any n that fits in the universe, alpha(n) <= 4. So treat it as constant time
and write O(m) or O(n + m)

10.1 The problem
Given a connected undirected weighted graph, choose a subset of edges that
1. keeps everything connected, and
2. has the smallest possible total weight.
Such a subset is always a tree on all n vertices: it has exactly n - 1 edges and no cycles. If it had a

minimum spanning tree, MST.

11.4.1 The idea
Keep a set of vertices whose distance is already final. Repeatedly take the unfinished vertex with the
smallest tentative distance, declare it final, and relax its outgoing edges.
Why is the smallest tentative distance final? Because all weights are non-negative, so any other route
to it would have to pass through some unfinished vertex first, which already has a larger tentative
distance, and adding non-negative weights cannot make it smaller. That argument fails the moment
a weight is negative, which is why Dijkstra requires non-negative weights.

If any edge can still be relaxed after n - 1 rounds, some path is getting shorter forever, which means
a negative cycle is reachable from the source. To find which vertices are affected, run one more
round and mark every vertex you improve, then propagate that mark along all outgoing edges with a

13.4 Articulation points
An articulation point (cut vertex) is a vertex whose removal increases the number of components.
Two rules, because the root of the DFS is special:
• For a non-root vertex u: it is an articulation point if it has a child v with low[v] >= tin[u]. Note
>=, not >. The subtree of v cannot get above u, so removing u cuts it off.
• For the root: it is an articulation point if and only if it has more than one child in the DFS tree.
With two or more children, the root is the only thing joining them.

13.5.1 Kosaraju’s algorithm
Two DFS passes, and it is the easiest SCC algorithm to remember.
1. Run DFS on the graph. Push each vertex onto a list when it FINISHES.
2. Reverse every edge.
3. Process vertices in reverse finish order. Each DFS on the reversed graph
that starts from an unvisited vertex marks exactly one SCC.

Build radj while reading the input: for every edge u -> v, push v into adj[u] and u into radj[v].
Why does it work? Intuition rather than proof: the vertex that finishes last in the first pass lies in a
“source” SCC of the condensation, one with no incoming edges from other components. Starting a
DFS from it in the reversed graph can only reach vertices of its own SCC, because the reversed edges
to other components point away . Peel that component off and repeat.
Time O(n + m), space O(n + m).

Ask these in order, on any problem that smells like a graph.
1. What are the vertices? Cities, cells, people, states of a process, positions plus extra information.
Write it down explicitly . If you cannot name the vertex set in one sentence, you have not modelled the

2. What are the edges, and what does one edge mean? “An edge means I can move from A to B in

14.2.5 5. Node splitting
A constraint on a vertex (a capacity , a cost to pass through, a limit on visits) cannot be expressed with
edge weights. Split the vertex into v_in and v_out, joined by an edge carrying the vertex’s property .
All original incoming edges go to v_in, all outgoing edges leave v_out.
14.2.6 6. Super source and super sink
“You may start from any of these k vertices” becomes: add vertex 0, join it to each of the k with weight
0, run a single search from 0.

and super sink
“You may start from any of these k vertices” becomes: add vertex 0, join it to each of the k with weight
0, run a single search from 0. Same for “you may finish at any of these”.
The MST version of this trick, where a vertex represents “build your own power plant”, was in Part 10.
14.2.7 7. Reverse the graph
“What is the distance from every vertex to vertex t” is not a single-source problem, until you reverse
every edge and run a single search from t. This turns an n-times problem into a once problem. Reach
for it whenever the target is fixed and the source varies.
14.2.8 8. Complement graph
Sometimes the graph you need is the complement of the given one, and the given one is dense while
the complement is sparse. There is a standard technique using a set of unvisited vertice

complement of the given one, and the given one is dense while
the complement is sparse. There is a standard technique using a set of unvisited vertices during BFS,
which keeps the total work at O(n + m). Know it exists.
14.2.9 9. Dependencies become a DAG
“A must come before B”, “you must learn X before Y”, “the letters are in some unknown alphabet
order”. Build an edge for each constraint and topologically sort. If the sort fails, the constraints

model example.

14.6 When you are stuck
In order:
1. Draw a small case, 5 or 6 vertices, and solve it by hand. Then ask what you did.
2. Say the vertex set out loud. “A vertex is a cell together with the direction I am facing.” If you
cannot finish that sentence, that is the blocker.
3

Say the vertex set out loud. “A vertex is a cell together with the direction I am facing.” If you
cannot finish that sentence, that is the blocker.
3. Count the states. If it is 1012, your model is wrong, not your code.
4. Look at the constraints again. n <= 500 with q queries screams Floyd. n <= 20 screams
bitmask. m <= 2*105 screams O(m log n).
5. Check whether a transformation makes it standard: reverse, super source, split, condense.
6. Ask what makes it non-standard, and put that thing into the state.

Part 1
Graph Fundamentals
Vocabulary, and how a graph differs from a tree
1.1 Why graphs exist
A tree can express hierarchy: one parent, many children, no way back up except the way you came.
That is a strong restriction, and most real relationships break it.
• Cities joined by roads. A city has no parent. You can drive in a circle.
• Friendships. If A is a friend of B then B is a friend of A. Not a hierarchy .
• Course prerequisites. Many courses depend on many others, and the dependency has a direction.
• Web pages linking to each other. Circular links are normal.
• States of a puzzle, where a move takes you from one state to another.
A graph is the most general “things and connections between them” structure. Trees, linked lists, grids

A graph is the most general “things and connections between them” structure. Trees, linked lists, grids
and hierarchies are all special cases of it. That generality is exactly why graphs are the single largest
topic in competitive programming.
1.2 Definition
A graph is a pair G = (V, E):
• V is a set of vertices, also called nodes. We number them 1 to n.
• E is a set of edges, each edge joining two vertices.
That is the whole definition. There is no root, no parent, no order among the neighbours of a vertex,
and no guarantee that everything is connected.

1.3 Terminology
Everything below refers to G1.
Vertex (plural vertices): a single item. Also called a node.
Edge: a connection. We write it 1-2 for undirected and 1->2 for directed.
Adjacent: two vertices joined by an edge. 1 and 2 are adjacent. 1 and 3 are not.
Neighbour: same thing from one vertex’s point of view. The neighbours of 2 are 1, 3, 4, 5.
Degree of a vertex: how many edges touch it. deg(2) = 4, deg(6) = 1, deg(7) = 1.
Handshake lemma: the sum of all degrees equals 2m, because every edge adds one to the degree of
each of its two endpoints. For G1: 2 + 4 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 16 = 2 * 8. Useful for checking
that you read the input correctly , and for the fact that the total work of visiting all adjacency lists is
O(m), not O(nm).

that you read the input correctly , and for the fact that the total work of visiting all adjacency lists is
O(m), not O(nm).
Walk: any sequence of vertices where consecutive ones are joined by an edge. Repeats allowed.
Path: a walk with no repeated vertex. 1 - 2 - 3 - 6 is a path.
Cycle: a path that returns to its starting vertex, using at least 3 distinct vertices in an undirected
graph. 1 - 2 - 4 - 1 is a cycle.
Connected: two vertices are connected if some path joins them. 1 and 6 are connected. 1 and 7 are
not.
Connected component: a maximal group of mutually connected vertices. G1 has two components:
{1,2,3,4,5,6} and {7,8}.
Simple graph: no self loops (an edge from a vertex to itself) and no multiple edges between the same

{1,2,3,4,5,6} and {7,8}.

between two cities” is a real sentence that appears in real problems.
Subgraph: some of the vertices plus some of the edges among them.
Sparse graph: m is close to n. Dense graph: m is close to n 2. This decides your representation, as
Part 2 explains.

only in its direction.

The four practical consequences, and you should write them on the first page of your notebook:
1. Always keep a visited array. Without it, DFS on a cyclic graph never terminates.
2. Always loop over all vertices when you want to cover the whole graph, because one DFS only
covers one component.

2. Always loop over all vertices when you want to cover the whole graph, because one DFS only
covers one component.
3. Complexity is O(n + m), not O(n). You touch every vertex once and every adjacency entry once,
and every undirected edge appears in two lists.
4. Recursion can go n deep. With n = 2 * 105 and heavy stack frames, plain DFS can crash. Keep
the frame small, or write it iteratively .
A tree is not a different data structure from a graph. A tree is a connected undirected graph with
no cycles, equivalently a connected graph with exactly n - 1 edges. Part 12 revisits the whole trees
course in graph language, and everything you learned there still works.
1.7 Families of graphs worth naming

1.7 Families of graphs worth naming
Tree: connected, acyclic, n - 1 edges, unique path between any two vertices. Adding any edge creates
exactly one cycle, and removing any edge disconnects it.
Forest: a disjoint set of trees. If a graph has c components, no cycles and n vertices, it has exactly n -
c edges.
DAG, directed acyclic graph: directed, no directed cycle. Every DAG has at least one vertex of indegree
0. This is the family where topological sorting and DP on the graph live (Part 8).
Bipartite graph: the vertices split into two sides so that every edge goes between the sides, never
inside one side. Equivalently , no odd cycle (Part 7).

inside one side. Equivalently , no odd cycle (Part 7).
Complete graph K_n: every pair joined. It has n(n-1)/2 edges, which is the maximum for a simple
undirected graph. A directed simple graph maxes out at n(n-1).
Grid graph: an r by c board where each cell is a vertex joined to its 4 (or 8) neighbours. Almost
never given as an edge list, so Part 2 shows the standard trick.
Functional graph: every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge, for example a[i] meaning “i points
to a[i]”. Such a graph is a set of cycles, each with trees hanging off it. Permutations are the special
case where it is exactly a set of cycles.

Implicit or state graph: the vertices are states of some process (a configuration of a puzzle, a position
plus a remaining fuel amount) and the edges are legal moves. You never build the graph, you generate
neighbours on demand. Part 14 is largely about spotting these.

If n and m are both up to 2 * 105, an adjacency matrix would need 4 * 1010 cells. That is not a close

1.9 Common mistakes
• Adding an undirected edge only once. Half your edges silently vanish.
• Forgetting visited. Infinite recursion, or exponential blowup on graphs with many cycles.
• Running one DFS from vertex 1 and assuming the graph is covered. Only true if the graph is
connected, and the statement must say so.
• Sizing arrays with n instead of n + 1 when vertices are numbered 1 to n.
• Using an adjacency matrix when n is 105.
• Assuming there is a path. In a disconnected graph the answer is often “-1”, and problems test
exactly that case.

• Assuming there is a path. In a disconnected graph the answer is often “-1”, and problems test
exactly that case.
• Assuming the graph is simple. Self loops and multiple edges break naive cycle detection.
• Assuming a connected graph with n vertices and n - 1 edges is a tree without checking
connectivity. You need both facts, though either one plus acyclicity implies the other.
• Ignoring that m can be 0.

3.7 Recursion depth, the practical danger
In a binary tree, recursion went as deep as the height, and a balanced tree gave you 20 frames. In a
graph, a simple path

gives you 200000 nested calls. Each frame holds the parameters, saved registers and the iterator over
the adjacency list. Typical stack limit on Codeforces is 256 MB, and plain DFS usually survives, but
code with large local arrays inside the recursive function will not.
Rules that keep you safe:
• Never declare a big local array inside a recursive function. Use globals.

4.1 What BFS does
Same as the level order traversal from the trees course: finish everything at distance 1, then everything
at distance 2, and so on. The queue is the same queue.
The difference from trees is again the visited check, and the payoff is bigger here, because BFS on a
graph answers a question DFS cannot:
In an unweighted graph, BFS from s gives the minimum number of edges from s to
every other vertex.
That sentence is the reason BFS matters. Memorise it with its condition: unweighted. The moment
edges have different weights, BFS is wrong and you need Part 11.
4.2 Why the layers are shortest distances
BFS processes vertices in non-decreasing order of distance. The argument is short enough to keep in
your head:

BFS processes vertices in non-decreasing order of distance. The argument is short enough to keep in
your head:
• Layer 0 is {s}, at distance 0, obviously correct.
• Suppose every vertex at distance k has been placed in the queue and nothing further has been.
When we pop those vertices and push their unvisited neighbours, any such neighbour must be at
distance exactly k + 1: it cannot be closer, or it would already have been found in an earlier layer,
and it is reachable in k + 1 steps by construction.
So the first time BFS reaches a vertex, it reaches it optimally. That is why we set dist and mark
visited at push time, not at pop time.

4.10 Common mistakes
• Marking visited when popping instead of when pushing. The same vertex enters the queue
many times. On a dense graph this is a real time limit failure, and in variants that count things it
is a wrong answer.
• Using BFS on a weighted graph. BFS counts edges, not weights. If the weights are not all equal,
the answer is wrong. This is the single most common conceptual error in shortest path problems.

• Forgetting the unreachable case. dist[t] == -1 must be handled and is always in the tests.
• Using vector with erase(begin()) as a queue. That is O(n) per pop.
• Reading g[nx][ny] before the bounds check. C++ will happily read out of bounds.
• Recomputing q.size() inside a loop condition when doing level by level processing. Snapshot
it, exactly as in the trees course.
• Running a separate BFS per source when multi-source BFS does it in one pass.
• Pushing the source without setting dist[s] = 0 . Then the source looks unvisited and gets
rediscovered.

7.2 The theorem
A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of odd length.
The forward direction is easy to see. Walk along a cycle: the colour alternates at every step, so to
come back to the starting vertex with the starting colour, the number of steps must be even.

8.2.2 Cycle detection, free of charge

is no recursion depth risk.

9.1 The problem it solves
You have n items, initially all separate. Two operations arrive in any order, many times:

With both improvements, m operations on n elements cost O(m alpha(n)), where alpha is the inverse

10.1 The problem
Given a connected undirected weighted graph, choose a subset of edges that
1. keeps everything connected, and

Such a subset is always a tree on all n vertices: it has exactly n - 1 edges and no cycles. If it had a

minimum spanning tree, MST.
Typical phrasing in problems: connect all cities with roads at minimum cost; lay cable so every house
has power; make the network connected as cheaply as possible.

11.4 3. Non-negative weights: Dijkstra
11.4.1 The idea
Keep a set of vertices whose distance is already final. Repeatedly take the unfinished vertex with the
smallest tentative distance, declare it final, and relax its outgoing edges.
Why is the smallest tentative distance final? Because all weights are non-negative, so any other route
to it would have to pass through some unfinished vertex first, which already has a larger tentative
distance, and adding non-negative weights cannot make it smaller. That argument fails the moment
a weight is negative, which is why Dijkstra requires non-negative weights.

11.5.3 Detecting a negative cycle
If any edge can still be relaxed after n - 1 rounds, some path is getting shorter forever, which means
a negative cycle is reachable from the source. To find which vertices are affected, run one more
round and mark every vertex you improve, then propagate that mark along all outgoing edges with a
BFS or DFS.
Time O(n m). Space O(n + m).
That complexity is why Bellman-Ford is the last resort. With n and m both 105 it is 1010 operations and
hopeless. It is used when n is small, or when negative weights genuinely appear (currency arbitrage,
profit and cost mixed together).

13.4 Articulation points
An articulation point (cut vertex) is a vertex whose removal increases the number of components.
Two rules, because the root of the DFS is special:
• For a non-root vertex u: it is an articulation point if it has a child v with low[v] >= tin[u]. Note
>=, not >. The subtree of v cannot get above u, so removing u cuts it off.

Why >= here and > for bridges? For a bridge we need the subtree to be unable to reachu at all. For
an articulation point it is enough that the subtree cannot get strictly above u, because u itself is being
deleted.
13.5 Strongly connected components
Now directed graphs. In a directed graph, “connected” splits in two:
• Weakly connected: connected if you ignore the directions.
• Strongly connected: every vertex can reach every other vertex, following the directions.
A strongly connected component (SCC) is a maximal set of vertices that can all reach each other.

13.6 Common mistakes
• Using low[v] instead of tin[v] on a back edge. The classic.
• Using > instead of >= for articulation points, or the reverse for bridges.
• Forgetting the special rule for the root.
• Skipping the parent by vertex when multi-edges exist. Skip by edge index.
• Forgetting to run the outer loop over all vertices on a disconnected graph.
• Building the reversed graph incorrectly in Kosaraju, most often by reversing only some edges.
• Assuming the condensation might have a cycle. It cannot.
• Recursion depth. These are all DFS, so a 2 * 105 chain is a real risk.

Part 14
How to Think About Graph Problems
Modelling first, algorithm second
This is the most important part of the course. Everything before it was equipment.
In a contest, the hard part is almost never “implement Dijkstra”. You can do that. The hard part is
noticing that the problem is a shortest path problem, and working out what the vertices are.
14.1 The ten questions
Ask these in order, on any problem that smells like a graph.
1. What are the vertices? Cities, cells, people, states of a process, positions plus extra information.
Write it down explicitly . If you cannot name the vertex set in one sentence, you have not modelled the
problem yet.
2. What are the edges, and what does one edge mean? “An edge means I can move from A to B in
one step.” One step of what?

2. What are the edges, and what does one edge mean? “An edge means I can move from A to B in
one step.” One step of what?
3. Directed or undirected? Look for the word “one-way”, or an asymmetric relation. When in doubt,
ask whether the relation is symmetric.
4. Weighted or unweighted? Are all moves equally expensive? If yes, BFS. If the costs are 0 and 1,
deque. Otherwise Dijkstra.
5. Are there cycles? If the relation is “must happen before”, the graph should be a DAG, and a cycle
means the answer is “impossible”. That is often the entire problem.
6. What is being asked: reachability, distance, ordering, connectivity, or structure?
reachability -> DFS or BFS
distance -> BFS, 0-1 BFS, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd
ordering -> topological sort
connectivity -> components, DSU

7. How big is the graph? n and m decide whether O(n3), O(m log n) or O(n + m) is allowed. And if
the vertices are states, count the states before you build anything.
8. Is the graph explicit or implicit? An explicit graph is given as an edge list. An implicit graph
(grid, states, i -> a[i]) is generated on demand. Most of the hard modelling problems are implicit.
9. Does the state need more than the vertex? “Shortest path, but you may make up to k edges free”
is not a graph on n vertices. It is a graph on n * (k+1) states. This is the single most valuable idea in
this part.

14.2.1 1. Explicit graph
The statement gives n, m and the edges. Read it in, pick an algorithm. Nothing to model.
14.2.2 2. Grid
Cells are vertices, adjacent free cells are edges. Never build the adjacency list, use the dx/dy loop

that change direction (state expansion, see below).

The vertices are configurations, the edges are legal moves. The classic examples:

The vertices are configurations, the edges are legal moves. The classic examples:
"minimum button presses to turn number x into y"

edges = the operations, each costing 1

14.2.5 5. Node splitting
A constraint on a vertex (a capacity , a cost to pass through, a limit on visits) cannot be expressed with
edge weights. Split the vertex into v_in and v_out, joined by an edge carrying the vertex’s property .

edge weights. Split the vertex into v_in and v_out, joined by an edge carrying the vertex’s property .
All original incoming edges go to v_in, all outgoing edges leave v_out.
14.2.6 6. Super source and super sink
“You may start from any of these k vertices” becomes: add vertex 0, join it to each of the k with weight
0, run a single search from 0. Same for “you may finish at any of these”.
The MST version of this trick, where a vertex represents “build your own power plant”, was in Part 10.
14.2.7 7. Reverse the graph
“What is the distance from every vertex to vertex t” is not a single-source problem, until you reverse
every edge and run a single search from t. This turns an n-times problem into a once problem. Reach
for it whenever the target is fixed and the source varies.

for it whenever the target is fixed and the source varies.
14.2.8 8. Complement graph
Sometimes the graph you need is the complement of the given one, and the given one is dense while
the complement is sparse. There is a standard technique using a set of unvisited vertices during BFS,
which keeps the total work at O(n + m). Know it exists.
14.2.9 9. Dependencies become a DAG
“A must come before B”, “you must learn X before Y”, “the letters are in some unknown alphabet
order”. Build an edge for each constraint and topologically sort. If the sort fails, the constraints
contradict each other, and reporting that is usually the point of the problem. Codeforces 510C is the
model example.
14.2.10 10. Equivalence becomes DSU

model example.
14.2.10 10. Equivalence becomes DSU
“These two are interchangeable”, “swap positions i and j freely”, “these accounts belong to the same
person”. Union them all, then work per group. The moment a problem says “and this relation is
transitive”, it is DSU.

How to Think About Graph Problems 92
14.2.11 11. Two options per item becomes 2-colouring
“Each person joins one of two teams and enemies must be separated” is bipartiteness. If the constraints
get more complicated (“if A is in team 1 then B must be in team 2”), you are looking at 2-SAT, which
is implication edges plus SCC. That is beyond this course, but Part 13 gave you its machinery .
14.2.12 12. i -> a[i] is a functional graph
An array of pointers, a permutation, “the winner of match i plays match a[i]”. Every vertex has
outdegree 1, so the structure is always a set of cycles with trees hanging off them. Questions about
“eventually you come back” are about the cycle.

14.5 Three worked examples
14.5.1 Example A
“There are n cities and m one-way roads. You start in city 1. Find the minimum number of
roads you must reverse so that city n becomes reachable.”
• Vertices: cities. Edges: roads.
• Directed. Weighted? Not stated, but reversing costs something.
• The move: use a road forwards for free, or backwards at a cost of 1.
• So build two edges per road: u -> v with weight 0, and v -> u with weight 1.
• Weights are 0 and 1, so this is 0-1 BFS. O(n + m).
Question 2 (“what does one edge mean”) did all the work.

14.5.2 Example B
“A grid with walls. You may break at most k walls. Find the minimum number of steps
from the top left to the bottom right.”
• The vertex is not a cell. Two visits to the same cell are different if you have broken different
numbers of walls.
• State: (row, column, walls broken so far). Size R * C * (k + 1).

14.6 When you are stuck
In order:
1. Draw a small case, 5 or 6 vertices, and solve it by hand. Then ask what you did.
2. Say the vertex set out loud. “A vertex is a cell together with the direction I am facing.” If you
cannot finish that sentence, that is the blocker.
3. Count the states. If it is 1012, your model is wrong, not your code.

3. Count the states. If it is 1012, your model is wrong, not your code.
4. Look at the constraints again. n <= 500 with q queries screams Floyd. n <= 20 screams
bitmask. m <= 2*105 screams O(m log n).
5. Check whether a transformation makes it standard: reverse, super source, split, condense.
6. Ask what makes it non-standard, and put that thing into the state.
14.7 Habits of strong contestants
• They write the vertex definition as a comment before writing code.
• They compute the state count and compare it with the time limit before implementing.
• They test on: a disconnected graph, a single vertex, a self loop if allowed, and the largest n.
• They use long long for any sum of weights, by default.

• They keep a personal template file with DSU, Dijkstra, BFS and the DFS skeletons, so implementa-

1.1 Why graphs exist
A tree can express hierarchy: one parent, many children, no way back up except the way you came. That is a strong restriction, and most real relationships break it.
• Cities joined by roads. A city has no parent. You can drive in a circle.
• Friendships. If A is a friend of B then B is a friend of A. Not a hierarchy .
• Course prerequisites. Many courses depend on many others, and the dependency has a direction.
• Web pages linking to each other. Circular links are normal.
• States of a puzzle, where a move takes you from one state to another.

Circular links are normal.
• States of a puzzle, where a move takes you from one state to another. A graph is the most general “things and connections between them” structure. Trees, linked lists, grids
and hierarchies are all special cases of it. That generality is exactly why graphs are the single largest
topic in competitive programming. 1.2 Definition
A graph is a pair G = (V, E):
• V is a set of vertices, also called nodes. We number them 1 to n.
• E is a set of edges, each edge joining two vertices. That is the whole definition. There is no root, no parent, no order among the neighbours of a vertex,
and no guarantee that everything is connected. 1 ------- 2 ------- 3

Everything below refers to G1. Vertex (plural vertices): a single item. Also called a node. Edge: a connection. We write it 1-2 for undirected and 1->2 for directed. BFS processes vertices in non-decreasing order of distance. The argument is short enough to keep in

The argument is short enough to keep in

• Layer 0 is {s}, at distance 0, obviously correct.
• Suppose every vertex at distance k has been placed in the queue and nothing further has been. When we pop those vertices and push their unvisited neighbours, any such neighbour must be at

• Assign dist[v] at push time. If you instead assign it when popping, the same vertex can be
pushed by several neighbours before it is popped, and you get duplicates in the queue, wasted

10.1 The problem
Given a connected undirected weighted graph, choose a subset of edges that
1. keeps everything connected, and
2. has the smallest possible total weight. Such a subset is always a tree on all n vertices: it has exactly n - 1 edges and no cycles. If it had a
cycle you could delete an edge of that cycle and stay connected while paying less. Hence the name
minimum spanning tree, MST. Typical phrasing in problems: connect all cities with roads at minimum cost; lay cable so every house
has power; make the network connected as cheaply as possible.

Typical phrasing in problems: connect all cities with roads at minimum cost; lay cable so every house
has power; make the network connected as cheaply as possible. If the graph is disconnected there is no spanning tree. Then the answer is usually a minimum
spanning forest, one tree per component, and the problem will say so or will guarantee connectivity . 10.2 The working example, G3

11.5.3 Detecting a negative cycle
If any edge can still be relaxed after n - 1 rounds, some path is getting shorter forever, which means
a negative cycle is reachable from the source. To find which vertices are affected, run one more
round and mark every vertex you improve, then propagate that mark along all outgoing edges with a
BFS or DFS. Time O(n m). Space O(n + m). That complexity is why Bellman-Ford is the last resort. With n and m both 105 it is 1010 operations and
hopeless. It is used when n is small, or when negative weights genuinely appear (currency arbitrage,
profit and cost mixed together). SPFA is a queue-based optimisation of Bellman-Ford that is usually fast but has a worst case of O(n
m), and Codeforces problem setters have written anti-SPFA tests.

13.5.1 Kosaraju’s algorithm
Two DFS passes, and it is the easiest SCC algorithm to remember. 1. Run DFS on the graph. Push each vertex onto a list when it FINISHES. 2. Reverse every edge. 3. Process vertices in reverse finish order.
Process vertices in reverse finish order.

Why does it work? Intuition rather than proof: the vertex that finishes last in the first pass lies in a
“source” SCC of the condensation, one with no incoming edges from other components. Starting a
DFS from it in the reversed graph can only reach vertices of its own SCC, because the reversed edges
to other components point away . Peel that component off and repeat. Time O(n + m), space O(n + m). Tarjan’s algorithm does the same in a single pass usinglow values, similar in spirit to bridges. It is
faster by a constant factor and harder to recall under pressure. Learn Kosaraju first. 13.5.2 The condensation graph

yes -> BFS (expand the state if the answer needs more than a position)

14.3 The decision guide
Is the answer "minimum number of moves" and every move costs the same?
yes -> BFS (expand the state if the answer needs more than a position)
Are there weights?

0/1 -> deque BFS
non-negative -> Dijkstra
negative -> Bellman-Ford
all pairs, n small -> Floyd
Is it "who must come before whom", or "is this possible without contradiction"?
-> topological sort on a DAG, and a failed sort means a cycle
Is it "are these two in the same group", especially with edges arriving over time?
-> DSU
Is it "connect everything as cheaply as possible"?
-> MST
Is it "which single edge or vertex breaks the graph"?
-> bridges and articulation points
Is it a directed graph where cycles are getting in the way?
-> SCC, then work on the condensation DAG
Is it a tree, and the question is about paths or subtrees?
-> root it, subtree DP, LCA

14.5 Three worked examples
14.5.1 Example A
“There are n cities and m one-way roads.

You start in city 1. Find the minimum number of
roads you must reverse so that city n becomes reachable.”
• Vertices: cities. Edges: roads.
• Directed. Weighted? Not stated, but reversing costs something.
• The move: use a road forwards for free, or backwards at a cost of 1.
• So build two edges per road: u -> v with weight 0, and v -> u with weight 1.
• Weights are 0 and 1, so this is 0-1 BFS. O(n + m). Question 2 (“what does one edge mean”) did all the work. 14.5.2 Example B
“A grid with walls. You may break at most k walls. Find the minimum number of steps
from the top left to the bottom right.”
• The vertex is not a cell. Two visits to the same cell are different if you have broken different
numbers of walls.
• State: (row, column, walls broken so far).

Two visits to the same cell are different if you have broken different
numbers of walls.
• State: (row, column, walls broken so far). Size R * C * (k + 1).
• Every move costs 1, so BFS on states.
• dist[R][C][k+1], and moving into a wall increases the third coordinate. Question 9 did all the work. 14.5.3 Example C
“n people, and m statements of the form ‘i and j are the same species’. Then q queries
asking whether two people are the same species.”

--- Page Break ---

How to Think About Graph Problems 94
• No distances, no ordering. Just “same group”, and the relation is transitive.
• DSU.

Just “same group”, and the relation is transitive.
• DSU. Union each statement, answer each query with find(a) == find(b).
• If the statements could also say “i and j are different species, and there are exactly two species”, it
becomes bipartite checking, or DSU with parity . Question 6 did all the work. 14.6 When you are stuck
In order:
1. Draw a small case, 5 or 6 vertices, and solve it by hand. Then ask what you did. 2. Say the vertex set out loud. “A vertex is a cell together with the direction I am facing.” If you
cannot finish that sentence, that is the blocker. 3. Count the states. If it is 1012, your model is wrong, not your code. 4. Look at the constraints again. n <= 500 with q queries screams Floyd. n <= 20 screams
bitmask. m <= 2*105 screams O(m log n). 5.

5. Check whether a transformation makes it standard: reverse, super source, split, condense. 6. Ask what makes it non-standard, and put that thing into the state. 14.7 Habits of strong contestants
• They write the vertex definition as a comment before writing code.
• They compute the state count and compare it with the time limit before implementing.
• They test on: a disconnected graph, a single vertex, a self loop if allowed, and the largest n.
• They use long long for any sum of weights, by default.
• They keep a personal template file with DSU, Dijkstra, BFS and the DFS skeletons, so implementa-
tion time goes to the modelling.
• They read the constraints before the statement. 14.8 Check yourself

Graphs and Graph Algorithms
A complete competitive programming course

Contents

How to Use This Material
0.1 Who this is for
Someone who has finished the Binary Trees course, or who is comfortable with recursion, vector,
queue, stack, map and basic complexity analysis, and who has never studied graphs.
The target is competitive programming. Everything here is written the way you would actually write
it in a contest: short, fast, 1-indexed, scanf-free but cin-with-fast-IO, global arrays where that is
simpler. Interview style is mentioned where it differs, but contests are the priority .
0.2 What you will be able to do at the end
Read a Codeforces problem, notice that it is a graph problem even when the word “graph” never
appears, build the graph, choose the right algorithm, and implement it correctly the first time.
Concretely, by the end you can solve most graph problems rated up to about 1600, and you will
understand the ideas behind harder ones.
The four questions this course trains you to ask:
What are the vertices, and what are the edges?
Is it directed? Is it weighted? Can it have cycles?
Do I need reachability, distance, ordering, or connectivity?
Which of the eight standard algorithms answers that question?
Modelling comes first. Half of all contest graph problems are easy once you see what the graph is,
and impossible before that.

Part 1
Graph Fundamentals
Vocabulary, and how a graph differs from a tree
1.1 Why graphs exist
A tree can express hierarchy: one parent, many children, no way back up except the way you came.
That is a strong restriction, and most real relationships break it.
• Cities joined by roads. A city has no parent. You can drive in a circle.
• Friendships. If A is a friend of B then B is a friend of A. Not a hierarchy .
• Course prerequisites. Many courses depend on many others, and the dependency has a direction.
• Web pages linking to each other. Circular links are normal.
• States of a puzzle, where a move takes you from one state to another.
A graph is the most general “things and connections between them” structure. Trees, linked lists, grids
and hierarchies are all special cases of it. That generality is exactly why graphs are the single largest
topic in competitive programming.
1.2 Definition
A graph is a pair G = (V, E):
• V is a set of vertices, also called nodes. We number them 1 to n.
• E is a set of edges, each edge joining two vertices.
That is the whole definition. There is no root, no parent, no order among the neighbours of a vertex,
and no guarantee that everything is connected.
1 ------- 2 ------- 3
| / | |
| / | |
| / | |
4 ------- 5 6
7 ------- 8
This is G1: n = 8, m = 8. Notice three things a tree would never allow: a cycle (1-2-4-1), a vertex
with four neighbours and no notion of “children”, and a second piece (7-8) not connected to the rest.
11

--- Page Break ---

Graph Fundamentals 12
1.3 Terminology
Everything below refers to G1.
Vertex (plural vertices): a single item. Also called a node.
Edge: a connection. We write it 1-2 for undirected and 1->2 for directed.
Adjacent: two vertices joined by an edge. 1 and 2 are adjacent. 1 and 3 are not.
Neighbour: same thing from one vertex’s point of view. The neighbours of 2 are 1, 3, 4, 5.
Degree of a vertex: how many edges touch it. deg(2) = 4, deg(6) = 1, deg(7) = 1.
Handshake lemma: the sum of all degrees equals 2m, because every edge adds one to the degree of
each of its two endpoints. For G1: 2 + 4 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 16 = 2 * 8. Useful for checking
that you read the input correctly , and for the fact that the total work of visiting all adjacency lists is
O(m), not O(nm).
Walk: any sequence of vertices where consecutive ones are joined by an edge. Repeats allowed.
Path: a walk with no repeated vertex. 1 - 2 - 3 - 6 is a path.
Cycle: a path that returns to its starting vertex, using at least 3 distinct vertices in an undirected
graph. 1 - 2 - 4 - 1 is a cycle.
Connected: two vertices are connected if some path joins them. 1 and 6 are connected. 1 and 7 are
not.
Connected component: a maximal group of mutually connected vertices. G1 has two components:
{1,2,3,4,5,6} and {7,8}.
Simple graph: no self loops (an edge from a vertex to itself) and no multiple edges between the same
pair. Most problems give simple graphs, but read the statement, because “there may be multiple roads
between two cities” is a real sentence that appears in real problems.
Subgraph: some of the vertices plus some of the edges among them.
Sparse graph: m is close to n. Dense graph: m is close to n 2. This decides your representation, as

Part 2 explains.
1.4 Directed and undirected
An undirected edge can be walked both ways. A directed edge (also called an arc) can be walked
only in its direction.
undirected directed
1 --- 2 1 --> 2
In a directed graph, degree splits in two:
• outdegree(v): number of edges leaving v
• indegree(v): number of edges entering v

Graph Fundamentals 13
For G2:
1 ---> 2 ---> 4 ---> 5
| ^ ^
| | |
+----> 3 -----+ |
| |
+----> 6 -----+
outdegree: 1:2 2:1 3:2 4:1 6:1 5:0
indegree : 1:0 2:1 3:1 4:2 6:1 5:2
The single most common bug in beginner graph code is storing an undirected edge only once. An
undirected edge must be pushed into both adjacency lists. Say it out loud every time you write
the input loop.
Directed graphs also complicate connectivity . In a directed graph, “u can reach v” does not imply “v
can reach u”, which is why we need the notion of strongly connected components in Part 13.
1.5 Weighted and unweighted
A weight is a number attached to an edge: length, cost, time, capacity . Unweighted means every edge
counts as 1.
This distinction decides your shortest path algorithm, and nothing else in the course:
unweighted -> BFS, O(n + m)
weights only 0 or 1 -> 0-1 BFS (deque), O(n + m)
non-negative weights -> Dijkstra, O(m log n)
any weights, may be < 0 -> Bellman-Ford, O(n m)
all pairs, small n -> Floyd-Warshall, O(n^3)
Learn that block now. In Part 11 you will only be filling in the details.
1.6 Graph versus tree
You have already studied binary trees. Almost everything transfers, with four changes that cause
almost all beginner bugs.
Tree (from the previous
course) General graph

adj[N]

vertex

predecessors
Cycles impossible possible, this is the big one

Graph Fundamentals 14

course) General graph
Revisiting a node cannot happen happens constantly , so you
need visited[]
Connectivity the whole tree is one piece may be several components,
so loop over all start vertices

The four practical consequences, and you should write them on the first page of your notebook:
1. Always keep a visited array. Without it, DFS on a cyclic graph never terminates.
2. Always loop over all vertices when you want to cover the whole graph, because one DFS only
covers one component.
3. Complexity is O(n + m), not O(n). You touch every vertex once and every adjacency entry once,
and every undirected edge appears in two lists.
4. Recursion can go n deep. With n = 2 * 105 and heavy stack frames, plain DFS can crash. Keep
the frame small, or write it iteratively .
A tree is not a different data structure from a graph. A tree is a connected undirected graph with
no cycles, equivalently a connected graph with exactly n - 1 edges. Part 12 revisits the whole trees
course in graph language, and everything you learned there still works.
1.7 Families of graphs worth naming
Tree: connected, acyclic, n - 1 edges, unique path between any two vertices. Adding any edge creates
exactly one cycle, and removing any edge disconnects it.
Forest: a disjoint set of trees. If a graph has c components, no cycles and n vertices, it has exactly n -
c edges.
DAG, directed acyclic graph: directed, no directed cycle. Every DAG has at least one vertex of indegree
0. This is the family where topological sorting and DP on the graph live (Part 8).
Bipartite graph: the vertices split into two sides so that every edge goes between the sides, never
inside one side. Equivalently , no odd cycle (Part 7).
Complete graph K_n: every pair joined. It has n(n-1)/2 edges, which is the maximum for a simple
undirected graph. A directed simple graph maxes out at n(n-1).
Grid graph: an r by c board where each cell is a vertex joined to its 4 (or 8) neighbours. Almost
never given as an edge list, so Part 2 shows the standard trick.
Functional graph: every vertex has exactly one outgoing edge, for example a[i] meaning “i points
to a[i]”. Such a graph is a set of cycles, each with trees hanging off it. Permutations are the special
case where it is exactly a set of cycles.

--- Page Break ---

Graph Fundamentals 15
Implicit or state graph: the vertices are states of some process (a configuration of a puzzle, a position
plus a remaining fuel amount) and the edges are legal moves. You never build the graph, you generate
neighbours on demand. Part 14 is largely about spotting these.
1.8 Reading the constraints
Contest constraints tell you the intended algorithm before you have read the statement properly .
n <= 20 bitmask over subsets, 2^n states
n <= 500 O(n^3) is fine: Floyd-Warshall, or an adjacency matrix
n <= 2000 O(n^2) or O(n m) on a sparse graph
n, m <= 2 * 10^5 O(n + m) or O(m log n). Adjacency list, nothing heavier
n <= 10^6 O(n + m) with fast IO, keep constants small
weights up to 10^9 sums need long long
If n and m are both up to 2 * 105, an adjacency matrix would need 4 * 1010 cells. That is not a close
call, it is impossible. Sparse means list.
1.9 Common mistakes
• Adding an undirected edge only once. Half your edges silently vanish.
• Forgetting visited. Infinite recursion, or exponential blowup on graphs with many cycles.
• Running one DFS from vertex 1 and assuming the graph is covered. Only true if the graph is
connected, and the statement must say so.
• Sizing arrays with n instead of n + 1 when vertices are numbered 1 to n.
• Using an adjacency matrix when n is 105.
• Assuming there is a path. In a disconnected graph the answer is often “-1”, and problems test
exactly that case.
• Assuming the graph is simple. Self loops and multiple edges break naive cycle detection.
• Assuming a connected graph with n vertices and n - 1 edges is a tree without checking
connectivity. You need both facts, though either one plus acyclicity implies the other.
• Ignoring that m can be 0.
1.10 Check yourself
1. G1 has 8 edges. What is the sum of all degrees, and why can you answer without adding them up
one by one?
2. A graph has n = 10 vertices and 3 components and no cycles. How many edges does it have?
3. Why does a general graph need a visited array when a binary tree traversal does not?
4. What is the maximum number of edges in a simple undirected graph on n vertices? On a directed
one?
5. The constraints say n <= 400 and there are queries asking for the distance between any two
vertices. Which algorithm is being hinted at?
6. Give a real-world relationship that is directed and one that is undirected.
7. Why is the traversal complexity O(n + m) and not O(n * m)?

Part 3
Depth First Search
The visited array, the DFS tree, entry and exit times
3.1 What DFS does
Same idea as in the trees course: go as deep as you can, and back up only when stuck. In a maze,
keep your hand on the left wall and walk.
The code even looks the same. Compare:
// tree version, from the previous course
void dfs(TreeNode* node) {
if (node == NULL) return;
dfs(node->left);
dfs(node->right);
}
// graph version
void dfs(int u) {
vis[u] = 1;
for (int v : adj[u])
if (!vis[v]) dfs(v);
}
Two differences, and they are the whole story:
1. A node had exactly two children. A vertex has any number of neighbours, so the two calls become
a loop.
2. A tree had no cycles, so you could never arrive twice at the same node. A graph can, so we need
vis[].
3.2 Why the visited array is not optional
Run the graph code on G1 withoutvis, starting at 1:
1 ------- 2
| /
| /
4 ----/
dfs(1) calls dfs(2), which calls dfs(1) (because 1 is a neighbour of 2), which callsdfs(2) again.
The program never stops. On a graph with cycles, no visited array means infinite recursion.
22

--- Page Break ---

Depth First Search 23
Even on an acyclic directed graph it is not safe to drop it. A DAG can force exponential work:
1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 6 ...
\ \ \
\--> 3 --> 5 ...
Without marking, the number of paths explored can double at every layer. vis[] turns “explore every
path” into “explore every vertex once”, which is the difference between exponential and linear.
3.3 Recursive DFS
const int N = 200005;
vector<int> adj[N];
bool vis[N];
void dfs(int u) {
vis[u] = true;
// work done on entering u (preorder position)
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (!vis[v]) {
dfs(v);
}
}
// work done on leaving u (postorder position)
}
The preorder and postorder positions are exactly the ones from the trees course, and they are used for
the same reasons: information flowing down goes in the first position, information coming back up
goes in the second.
Mark vis[u] = true on entry, before the loop, not after it. Marking after the loop means a cycle
re-enters u before it was marked, and you are back to infinite recursion.

| / | |
| / | |
4 ------- 5 6

look at 3 -> not visited

look at 6 -> not visited

Vertices 7 and 8 were never reached. One DFS explores one component, and nothing more. That is
the second big difference from trees.
3.4.1 The order depends on the adjacency order
If the input had listed edge 1-4 before 1-2, the order would have been 1 4 2 3 6 5. Both are valid
depth first orders. Never write a solution whose correctness depends on which neighbour comes
first, unless you sorted the lists on purpose (which some problems, such as lexicographically smallest
orderings, do require).
3.5 Covering the whole graph
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
if (!vis[i])
dfs(i);
Four lines that appear in half of all graph solutions. Wrapping a counter around them counts
components, which is Part 5.
3.6 Complexity
Time O(n + m).
The reason is worth stating properly , because students often guess O(n * m). Each vertex is entered at
most once, because of vis. When a vertex u is entered, the loop runs deg(u) times. So the total loop
work is the sum over all vertices ofdeg(u), which by the handshake lemma is2m for an undirected
graph and m for a directed one. Add the n entries and you get O(n + m).

--- Page Break ---

Depth First Search 25
Space O(n) for vis plus O(n) for the recursion stack in the worst case, on top of the O(n + m) the
graph itself occupies.
3.7 Recursion depth, the practical danger
In a binary tree, recursion went as deep as the height, and a balanced tree gave you 20 frames. In a
graph, a simple path
1 - 2 - 3 - 4 - ... - 200000
gives you 200000 nested calls. Each frame holds the parameters, saved registers and the iterator over
the adjacency list. Typical stack limit on Codeforces is 256 MB, and plain DFS usually survives, but
code with large local arrays inside the recursive function will not.
Rules that keep you safe:
• Never declare a big local array inside a recursive function. Use globals.
• Pass few parameters, and pass them by value if they are ints, or by reference if they are containers.
• If the problem has n up to 106, or you are on a judge with a small stack, write the iterative version.
3.8 Iterative DFS
void dfsIterative(int s) {
stack<int> st;
st.push(s);
while (!st.empty()) {
int u = st.top();
st.pop();
if (vis[u]) continue; // may have been pushed several times
vis[u] = true;
for (int v : adj[u])
if (!vis[v])
st.push(v);
}
}
Two subtleties:
1. A vertex can be pushed more than once, by different neighbours, before it is popped. So the
check if (vis[u]) continue; after popping is required. Marking at push time also works and
pushes fewer duplicates, but then the order of visits changes.
2. The visit order is not identical to the recursive version. The stack reverses the neighbour
order, so this code visits the last neighbour first. To match exactly , iterateadj[u] in reverse when
pushing. For most problems the order does not matter, but for a printed answer it does.
This simple version cannot do postorder work, because when you pop u you do not yet know when its
subtree finishes. If you need the postorder position (for topological sort or SCC), either use recursion,

--- Page Break ---

Depth First Search 26
or push pairs of (vertex, edge index) and simulate the call stack properly. Recursion is almost
always the better choice.
3.9 The DFS tree
Every DFS implicitly builds a tree: whenever dfs(u) calls dfs(v), draw a tree edge u - v. For G1
starting at 1:
DFS tree non-tree edges
1 1 - 4 (back edge)
| 2 - 5 (back edge)
2
/ \
3 4
| |
6 5
The component had 6 vertices and 7 edges. Five of them are tree edges (a tree on 6 vertices) and two
are left over.
In an undirected graph, every non-tree edge joins a vertex to one of its own ancestors. Such an edge
is called a back edge. There are no “cross edges” going sideways between different branches, and
this is not an accident: if such an edge existed, DFS would have walked along it and made it a tree
edge. That single fact is the foundation of cycle detection, bridges and articulation points.
In a directed graph, four kinds of non-tree edge are possible: back (to an ancestor), forward (to a
descendant), and cross (to an already-finished vertex elsewhere). Only back edges indicate a cycle.

Part 6 and Part 13 use this.
3.10 Entry and exit times
Give the DFS a clock. Record the time at which each vertex is entered and left.
int timer = 0;
int tin[N], tout[N];
void dfs(int u) {
vis[u] = true;
tin[u] = timer++;
for (int v : adj[u])
if (!vis[v]) dfs(v);
tout[u] = timer++;
}
On G1 from vertex 1:
vertex : 1 2 3 6 4 5
tin : 0 1 2 3 6 7

--- Page Break ---

Depth First Search 27
tout : 11 10 5 4 9 8
The pairs nest like brackets:
1 [ 2 [ 3 [ 6 [ ] ] 4 [ 5 [ ] ] ] ]
This gives you a genuinely useful test, in O(1):
u is an ancestor of v in the DFS tree if and only if tin[u] <= tin[v] and tout[v] <=
tout[u].
That single line is used for:
• checking ancestry without walking up the tree
• turning a subtree into a contiguous range of an array , so that subtree queries become range queries
(the Euler tour trick, mentioned again in Part 12)
• bridges and articulation points, in Part 13
It is worth spending five minutes drawing the bracket picture until it feels obvious.
3.11 What DFS is good for
connected components Part 5
cycle detection Part 6
bipartite checking (2-colouring) Part 7
topological sort Part 8
subtree sizes and tree DP Part 12
bridges, articulation points, SCC Part 13
flood fill on grids Part 5
counting paths in a DAG Part 8
What DFS is not good for: shortest paths in an unweighted graph. DFS finds a path, almost never the
shortest one. That is BFS, and it is the next part.
3.12 Common mistakes
• Marking vis[u] after the loop instead of before it. Infinite recursion.
• Only running DFS from vertex 1. Misses every other component.
• Not resetting vis between test cases, or resetting all 200005 entries every test and timing out.
• Believing DFS gives shortest paths. It does not.
• Declaring int cnt[100000] inside the recursive function. Stack death.
• Assuming the DFS order is unique. It depends on the input order of edges.
• In the iterative version, forgetting the if (vis[u]) continue; after popping.
• Using int for a timer in a problem with 106 vertices and then also using 2 * timer . Fine for
ints, but check.

Part 4
Breadth First Search
Shortest paths in unweighted graphs
4.1 What BFS does
Same as the level order traversal from the trees course: finish everything at distance 1, then everything
at distance 2, and so on. The queue is the same queue.
The difference from trees is again the visited check, and the payoff is bigger here, because BFS on a
graph answers a question DFS cannot:
In an unweighted graph, BFS from s gives the minimum number of edges from s to
every other vertex.
That sentence is the reason BFS matters. Memorise it with its condition: unweighted. The moment
edges have different weights, BFS is wrong and you need Part 11.
4.2 Why the layers are shortest distances
BFS processes vertices in non-decreasing order of distance. The argument is short enough to keep in
your head:
• Layer 0 is {s}, at distance 0, obviously correct.
• Suppose every vertex at distance k has been placed in the queue and nothing further has been.
When we pop those vertices and push their unvisited neighbours, any such neighbour must be at
distance exactly k + 1: it cannot be closer, or it would already have been found in an earlier layer,
and it is reachable in k + 1 steps by construction.
So the first time BFS reaches a vertex, it reaches it optimally. That is why we set dist and mark
visited at push time, not at pop time.
4.3 The code
vector<int> bfs(int s, int n, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
vector<int> dist(n + 1, -1); // -1 means unreached, and doubles as "not visited"
queue<int> q;
dist[s] = 0;
q.push(s);
29

--- Page Break ---

Breadth First Search 30
while (!q.empty()) {
int u = q.front();
q.pop();
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (dist[v] == -1) { // first time we see v
dist[v] = dist[u] + 1;
q.push(v);
}
}
}
return dist;
}
Eleven lines, and you will write them a hundred times. Learn them until they come out without
thinking.
Two design choices worth defending:
• One array instead of two. dist[v] == -1 already means “not visited”, so a separate vis array is
redundant and gives you one more thing to forget.
• Assign dist[v] at push time. If you instead assign it when popping, the same vertex can be
pushed by several neighbours before it is popped, and you get duplicates in the queue, wasted
work, and in some variants a wrong answer.

order visited : 1 2 4 3 5 6
dist : d[1]=0 d[2]=1 d[4]=1 d[3]=2 d[5]=2 d[6]=3
d[7], d[8] : still -1, different component
Compare with the DFS order from Part 3, which was1 2 3 6 4 5. DFS reached vertex 6 second-to-
last by diving; BFS reached it last because it is genuinely the farthest. DFS orders tell you nothing
about distance.
Time O(n + m), space O(n). Same argument as DFS: every vertex enters the queue at most once,
and each adjacency list is scanned once.
4.5 Reconstructing the path
Distance alone is often not enough. Record where each vertex was reached from.
vector<int> par(n + 1, 0);
// inside the loop, when you discover v:
dist[v] = dist[u] + 1;
par[v] = u;
q.push(v);
// afterwards, to print the path from s to t:
if (dist[t] == -1) {
cout << -1 << "\n"; // unreachable, this case is always tested
} else {
vector<int> path;
for (int cur = t; cur != 0; cur = par[cur]) path.push_back(cur);
reverse(path.begin(), path.end());
for (int v : path) cout << v << " ";
}
On G1, par[6] = 3, par[3] = 2, par[2] = 1, so the path 1 to 6 is1 2 3 6, of length 3, matching
dist[6].
Note par[s] = 0 acts as the stop marker, which is why 1-indexing is convenient here.
4.6 BFS on a grid
The grid is a graph, so BFS is BFS. Only the neighbour loop changes.
int R, C;
vector<string> g;

--- Page Break ---

Breadth First Search 32
int dx[4] = {-1, 1, 0, 0};
int dy[4] = { 0, 0,-1, 1};
vector<vector<int>> bfsGrid(int sx, int sy) {
vector<vector<int>> d(R, vector<int>(C, -1));
queue<pair<int,int>> q;
d[sx][sy] = 0;
q.push({sx, sy});
while (!q.empty()) {
auto [x, y] = q.front(); q.pop();
for (int k = 0; k < 4; k++) {
int nx = x + dx[k], ny = y + dy[k];
if (nx < 0 || nx >= R || ny < 0 || ny >= C) continue;
if (g[nx][ny] == '#') continue;
if (d[nx][ny] != -1) continue;
d[nx][ny] = d[x][y] + 1;
q.push({nx, ny});
}
}
return d;
}
On G4, starting from the top left cell:
grid distances from (0,0)
. . # . . 0 1 # 7 8
. # # . . 1 # # 6 7
. . . . . 2 3 4 5 6
# # . # . # # 5 # 7
The shortest route from the top left to the bottom right cell is 7 moves. Trace it: down, down, right,
right, right, right, down, which is (0,0) (1,0) (2,0) (2,1) (2,2) (2,3) (2,4) (3,4). Seven
moves, and the distance grid agrees.
Notice the top right corner is at distance 8 even though it looks close. The wall at (0,2) forces the
whole journey around the bottom. That is exactly the kind of thing BFS handles and eyeballing does
not.
4.7 Multi-source BFS
Question: given several starting cells, what is the distance from each cell to the nearest start?
The naive answer is to run one BFS per source, which is O(k(n + m)). The right answer is to push all
sources into the queue at the start with distance 0, and run a single BFS.
for (auto s : sources) {
dist[s] = 0;
q.push(s);
}

--- Page Break ---

Breadth First Search 33
// then the identical loop
Why is this correct? Imagine adding one imaginary super source S joined to every real source by an
edge of weight 0. BFS from S is exactly the loop above. Each vertex is labelled with its distance to the
nearest real source, in a single O(n + m) pass.
This appears constantly: “distance to the nearest 1 in a binary matrix”, “how long until fire reaches
every cell”, “minimum time for any of the guards to reach each room”. Whenever you see the word
nearest together with several starting points, this is the tool.
4.8 BFS from every component
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
if (dist[i] == -1)
bfsFrom(i);
Same shape as the DFS loop. Distances from different components are not comparable, so this pattern
is usually about components, not distances.
4.9 BFS or DFS
Question Use
Fewest edges, unweighted BFS
Distance to nearest of several sources multi-source BFS
Level by level processing BFS
Is there a path at all either, DFS is shorter to write
Connected components either
Cycle detection either, DFS is more natural
Topological sort either (Kahn is BFS, the other is DFS)
Bridges, articulation points, SCC DFS, they need the DFS tree
Subtree information, tree DP DFS
Graph is a chain of 106 vertices BFS, no recursion depth problem
Weighted shortest path neither, see Part 11
Rough rule: BFS answers “how far”, DFS answers “what is the structure”.
4.10 Common mistakes
• Marking visited when popping instead of when pushing. The same vertex enters the queue
many times. On a dense graph this is a real time limit failure, and in variants that count things it
is a wrong answer.
• Using BFS on a weighted graph. BFS counts edges, not weights. If the weights are not all equal,
the answer is wrong. This is the single most common conceptual error in shortest path problems.

--- Page Break ---

Breadth First Search 34
• Forgetting the unreachable case. dist[t] == -1 must be handled and is always in the tests.
• Using vector with erase(begin()) as a queue. That is O(n) per pop.
• Reading g[nx][ny] before the bounds check. C++ will happily read out of bounds.
• Recomputing q.size() inside a loop condition when doing level by level processing. Snapshot
it, exactly as in the trees course.
• Running a separate BFS per source when multi-source BFS does it in one pass.
• Pushing the source without setting dist[s] = 0 . Then the source looks unvisited and gets
rediscovered.
4.11 Codeforces problems that test exactly this
• 601A, The Two Routes. BFS on a graph and on its complement. https://codeforces.com/problem
set/problem/601/A
• 1130C, Connect. Two BFS runs plus a small brute force. https://codeforces.com/problemset/prob
lem/1130/C
• 1365D, Solve The Maze. Multi-source reasoning on a grid. https://codeforces.com/problemset/pr
oblem/1365/D
• 796D, Police Stations. Multi-source BFS on a tree. https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/
796/D
4.12 Check yourself
1. State the BFS theorem, including its condition.
2. Why must dist[v] be set at push time rather than pop time?
3. Give the BFS distances from vertex 3 in G1.
4. Why does pushing all sources at the start compute the distance to the nearest source?
5. On G4, why is the top right cell at distance 8 rather than 4?
6. You need the shortest path itself, not just its length. What extra array do you keep, and how do
you use it?
7. A problem has edge weights 1 and 5. Can you still use plain BFS? What would you do instead?

--- Page Break ---
