section_based.text:
Part 6
Cycle Detection
Undirected and directed, and why they are different problems
Cycles are the feature that separates graphs from trees, so detecting them is a basic skill. The
undirected case and the directed case need different code, and using one for the other is a classic
wrong answer.
6.1 Undirected graphs
6.1.1 The idea
Run a DFS. If you ever reach a vertex that is already visited and is not the neighbour you came
from, you have found a second way to get there, which closes a cycle.
The “not the one you came from” clause exists because in an undirected graph every edge appears in
both adjacency lists. Standing at 2 having come from 1, you will see 1 among your neighbours and it
will be visited. That is not a cycle, that is the edge you just walked.
1 ------- 2
| /
| /
4 ----/
dfs(1) -> dfs(2): from 2, neighbour 1 is visited but it is the parent, ignore
-> dfs(4) from 2: from 4, neighbour 1 is visited and is NOT the parent
=> cycle found: 1 - 2 - 4 - 1
6.1.2 Code
bool dfsCycle(int u, int parent, vector<vector<int>>& adj, vector<bool>& vis) {
vis[u] = true;
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (!vis[v]) {
if (dfsCycle(v, u, adj, vis)) return true ;
} else if (v != parent) {
return true ; // visited, and not where we came from
}
}
return false ;
}
bool hasCycle(int n, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
vector<bool> vis(n + 1, false);
40

--- Page Break ---

Cycle Detection 41
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
if (!vis[i] && dfsCycle(i, 0, adj, vis))
return true ;
return false ;
}
parent = 0 for the root of each DFS, which is why 1-indexing is convenient.
Time O(n + m), space O(n).
6.1.3 Dry run on G1
dfs(1, parent 0)
vis={1}, neighbours 2, 4
dfs(2, parent 1)
vis={1,2}, neighbours 1, 3, 4, 5
1 is visited and equals parent -> skip
dfs(3, parent 2)
neighbour 2 is visited and equals parent -> skip
dfs(6, parent 3): neighbour 3 is parent -> skip, return false
return false
dfs(4, parent 2)
neighbour 1: visited, and 1 != parent(2) => CYCLE
The cycle is 1 - 2 - 4 - 1, exactly the triangle in the picture.
6.1.4 The parent trick and its two traps
Multiple edges. If the input contains the edge1-2 twice, then standing at 2 you see 1 twice. Both are
“the parent”, so the code above reports no cycle, when in fact two parallel edges are a cycle of length
2. If a problem allows multi-edges, compare edge ids instead of vertices: pass the index of the edge
you arrived on and skip only that one.
Self loops. An edge v-v is a cycle by itself. The code above sees v as a visited non-parent neighbour
and correctly reports a cycle, but some variants of the code skip v == u, so check your version.
If the statement says “the graph is simple”, neither case can happen and the parent version is fine.
6.1.5 Printing the cycle
Keep a parent array and, when the back edgeu -> v is found, walk up from u to v:
int cycleStart = -1, cycleEnd = -1;
vector<int> par;
bool dfs(int u, int p, vector<vector<int>>& adj, vector<bool>& vis) {
vis[u] = true;
par[u] = p;
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (v == p) continue;
if (vis[v]) { cycleStart = v; cycleEnd = u; return true ; }
if (dfs(v, u, adj, vis)) return true ;
}
return false ;

--- Page Break ---

Cycle Detection 42
}
// afterwards:
vector<int> cycle;
cycle.push_back(cycleStart);
for (int v = cycleEnd; v != cycleStart; v = par[v]) cycle.push_back(v);
cycle.push_back(cycleStart);
reverse(cycle.begin(), cycle.end());
6.1.6 Counting your way out
For the single question “does this undirected graph contain a cycle”, you do not even need DFS. A
graph is a forest exactly when it has no cycle, and a forest with n vertices and c components has n -
c edges. So:
cycle exists <=> m > n - c
Compute c with the component counting from Part 5. This is often the fastest thing to write, and it
also gives you “how many extra edges beyond a forest”.
The same fact applies per component: a component with k vertices and exactly k edges contains
exactly one cycle.
6.1.7 The DSU method
Process every edge (u, v). If u and v are already in the same set, this edge closes a cycle. Otherwise
union them. That is Part 9, and it is the method to use when edges arrive one at a time.
6.2 Directed graphs
6.2.1 Why the undirected method fails
1 ---> 2
| |
v v
3 ---> 4
There is no directed cycle here: from 4 you cannot get back anywhere. But an undirected style DFS
starting at 1 would go 1 -> 2 -> 4, then from 1 go to 3, see 4 already visited and not the parent,
and shout “cycle”. Wrong.
The problem is that “already visited” is too coarse. What matters is whether the vertex is still on
the current recursion stack, that is, whether we are still inside its call. An edge to a vertex that is
finished is harmless. An edge to a vertex we are currently inside is a cycle.
6.2.2 Three colours
0 = white : not visited yet
1 = grey : currently on the recursion stack, we entered it and have not left
2 = black : completely finished, we have left it
A grey neighbour means a back edge, which means a directed cycle. A black neighbour is fine.

--- Page Break ---

Cycle Detection 43
vector<int> color; // 0 white, 1 grey, 2 black
bool dfs(int u, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
color[u] = 1; // grey: entering
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (color[v] == 1) return true ; // back edge -> cycle
if (color[v] == 0 && dfs(v, adj)) return true ;
}
color[u] = 2; // black: leaving
return false ;
}
bool hasDirectedCycle(int n, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
color.assign(n + 1, 0);
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
if (color[i] == 0 && dfs(i, adj))
return true ;
return false ;
}
Notice there is no parent parameter at all. In a directed graph, an edge back to the vertex you came
from is a genuine 2-cycle and must be reported.
6.2.3 Dry run on G2, which has no cycle
1 ---> 2 ---> 4 ---> 5
| ^ ^
| | |
+----> 3 -----+ |
| |
+----> 6 -----+
dfs(1): grey 1
dfs(2): grey 2
dfs(4): grey 4
dfs(5): grey 5, no outgoing, black 5
black 4
black 2
dfs(3): grey 3
4 is black -> fine, not a cycle
dfs(6): grey 6
5 is black -> fine
black 6
black 3
black 1
no cycle
That is the whole point: vertex 4 was visited twice as a target, and only the colour told us it was
harmless.
Now add the edge 5 -> 1 and rerun. When we are inside dfs(5), vertex 1 is grey, so we report a

--- Page Break ---

Cycle Detection 44
cycle immediately , which is correct:1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 5 -> 1.
6.2.4 Printing the directed cycle
Same technique: keep par[], and when you find a grey neighbour v from u, walk u, par[u],
par[par[u]], ... back to v.
6.2.5 The Kahn alternative
Topological sorting (Part 8) gives you cycle detection for free: run Kahn’s algorithm, and if fewer
than n vertices come out, the leftovers form at least one cycle. Many people prefer this because it is
iterative, so it cannot blow the stack, and it usually needs to be written anyway .
6.3 Summary table
Undirected Directed
Test visited neighbour that is not the parent neighbour that is grey
Extra state parent vertex (or parent edge id) 3-colour array
Trap multi-edges and self loops using the parent trick, which is wrong
Alternative DSU, or m > n - c Kahn’s algorithm counting output size
Complexity O(n + m) O(n + m)
6.4 Common mistakes
• Using the parent trick on a directed graph. Reports cycles that are not there.
• Using the colour method on an undirected graph without handling the parent. Every single
edge looks like a 2-cycle, because u -> v -> u is always available.
• Comparing parent vertices when the graph can have multiple edges. Compare edge ids.
• Only starting from vertex 1. A cycle may live in another component.
• Forgetting to set black on exit. Then finished vertices stay grey and every cross edge looks like a
cycle.
• Returning as soon as one DFS finishes instead of continuing the outer loop over all vertices.
6.5 Codeforces problems that test exactly this
• 977E, Cyclic Components. Undirected, degree based. https://codeforces.com/problemset/proble
m/977/E
• 510B, Fox And Two Dots. Cycle detection on a grid, with the parent rule. https://codeforces.com
/problemset/problem/510/B
• 1249B2, Books Exchange. Cycles in a permutation, which is the simplest directed cycle structure.
https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1249/B2
• For directed cycle detection in general, any topological sort problem from Part 8 works, because a
failed topological sort is exactly a cycle.

--- Page Break ---

Cycle Detection 45
6.6 Check yourself
1. Why do we skip the parent in the undirected version?
2. Give a graph where the parent trick wrongly reports “no cycle”, and say how to fix it.
3. Why is “already visited” not enough in a directed graph?
4. What do grey and black mean, precisely?
5. A graph has n = 10, m = 12 and 2 components. Does it contain a cycle? How do you know
without running anything?
6. In the directed version, why is there no parent parameter?
7. How would you print the cycle rather than just report its existence?

--- Page Break ---

Part 7
Bipartite Graphs
Two colouring and odd cycles
7.1 What bipartite means
A graph is bipartite if you can split the vertices into two groups so that every edge goes between
the groups, and no edge stays inside a group.
Equivalently, and this is the version you use in code: you can colour every vertex black or white so
that no edge joins two vertices of the same colour.
bipartite not bipartite
1 --- 2 1 --- 2
| | \ /
3 --- 4 3
colour 1,4 black the triangle needs 3 colours
colour 2,3 white
Real problems say it differently: split people into two teams so that no two enemies are on the same
team; assign each task to one of two machines so that conflicting tasks differ; check whether a relation
can be explained by two categories.
7.2 The theorem
A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of odd length.
The forward direction is easy to see. Walk along a cycle: the colour alternates at every step, so to
come back to the starting vertex with the starting colour, the number of steps must be even.
The other direction is what the algorithm proves constructively: if you try to two-colour with BFS or
DFS and never hit a conflict, the colouring you produced is a valid split.
For G1:
1 ------- 2 ------- 3
| / | |
| / | |
| / | |
4 ------- 5 6
46

--- Page Break ---

Bipartite Graphs 47
G1 contains the triangle 1 - 2 - 4 - 1, which has length 3, odd. So G1 is not bipartite. No amount
of cleverness will colour it.
Note the second component {7, 8} is bipartite on its own. A graph is bipartite only if every
component is.
7.3 Two colouring by BFS
// returns true if bipartite; colour[] holds 0/1 for each vertex, -1 if unvisited
bool isBipartite(int n, vector<vector<int>>& adj, vector<int>& color) {
color.assign(n + 1, -1);
for (int s = 1; s <= n; s++) {
if (color[s] != -1) continue; // already coloured, other component
color[s] = 0;
queue<int> q;
q.push(s);
while (!q.empty()) {
int u = q.front(); q.pop();
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (color[v] == -1) {
color[v] = color[u] ˆ 1; // opposite colour
q.push(v);
} else if (color[v] == color[u]) {
return false ; // conflict, odd cycle
}
}
}
}
return true ;
}
color[u] ˆ 1 flips 0 to 1 and 1 to 0. You can also write1 - color[u].
The outer loop matters: an uncoloured vertex means a new component, which must be started fresh
with colour 0.
Time O(n + m), space O(n).
7.3.1 The DFS version
Identical logic, shorter:
bool dfs(int u, int c, vector<vector<int>>& adj, vector<int>& color) {
color[u] = c;
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (color[v] == -1) {
if (!dfs(v, c ˆ 1, adj, color)) return false ;
} else if (color[v] == c) {
return false ;
}

--- Page Break ---

Bipartite Graphs 48
}
return true ;
}
Use BFS if the graph might be a chain of 105 vertices, DFS otherwise. There is no difference in the
answer.
7.3.2 Dry run on G1
start s = 1, color[1] = 0
pop 1: neighbours 2, 4
color[2] = 1, push
color[4] = 1, push
pop 2: neighbours 1(0, differs, ok), 3, 4, 5
color[3] = 0, push
vertex 4 already coloured 1, and color[2] is also 1 => CONFLICT
The conflict is on the edge2-4, which is exactly the edge that closes the odd cycle1 - 2 - 4 - 1.
When a problem asks you to output the offending cycle, this edge plus the BFS parent pointers give it
to you.
7.3.3 A bipartite example, traced
1 --- 2
| |
3 --- 4
adjacency: 1: 2 3 2: 1 4 3: 1 4 4: 2 3
color[1] = 0
pop 1: color[2] = 1, color[3] = 1
pop 2: 1 has colour 0, fine; color[4] = 0
pop 3: 1 fine; 4 already 0, and color[3] = 1, different, fine
pop 4: 2 and 3 both 1, and color[4] = 0, fine
bipartite. Side A = {1, 4}, side B = {2, 3}
The 4-cycle is even, so it colours fine. That is the theorem in one example.
7.4 Using the colouring afterwards
The colour array is usually more useful than the yes/no answer:
• The two sides are {v : color[v] == 0} and {v : color[v] == 1}. Codeforces 1176E asks you
to output the smaller side, which is at most n/2 vertices, and that is the entire problem.
• On a tree, two colouring is free and never fails, because a tree has no cycles at all. Colour by depth
parity: even depth is side 0, odd depth is side 1.
• Bipartite graphs are where matching algorithms live. That is beyond this course, but knowing the
word tells you which theory applies.

--- Page Break ---

Bipartite Graphs 49
7.5 Common mistakes
• Only running from vertex 1. Other components may be non-bipartite, or may need their own
starting colour.
• Using a visited array separate from color. Redundant. color[v] == -1 means unvisited.
• Checking the conflict only when discovering a new vertex. The conflict shows up on an edge to
an already coloured vertex, so the else if branch is where the answer is decided.
• Believing that “no odd cycle” needs to be checked separately. The colouring algorithm is the
check.
• Assuming a bipartite graph has equal sides. It does not.
• Forgetting that a graph with no edges is bipartite, and so is a single vertex.
7.6 Codeforces problems that test exactly this
• 862B, Mahmoud and Ehab and the bipartiteness. Colour a tree, then count. https://codeforces.c
om/problemset/problem/862/B
• 1176E, Cover it! Take the smaller BFS parity class. https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/
1176/E
• 1144F, Graph Without Long Directed Paths. Orient edges using a 2-colouring. https://codeforces.c
om/problemset/problem/1144/F
7.7 Check yourself
1. State the odd cycle theorem in both directions.
2. Why is every tree bipartite?
3. Which edge of G1 causes the conflict, and which cycle does it close?
4. Why must the outer loop restart the colour at 0 for each component?
5. In the code, which branch actually detects non-bipartiteness?
6. A graph is bipartite with sides of size 3 and 7. What is the maximum number of edges it can have?
7. How would you output the odd cycle itself when the check fails?

--- Page Break ---

Part 8
Topological Sort and DP on a DAG
Ordering by dependency
8.1 The problem
You have tasks, and some must be done before others. Print an order in which all of them can be
done.
1 ---> 2 ---> 4 ---> 5
| ^ ^
| | |
+----> 3 -----+ |
| |
+----> 6 -----+
That is G2. A valid order is 1 2 3 4 6 5: whenever there is an edge u -> v, u appears before v.
A topological order is exactly that: a linear order of all vertices such that every directed edge points
forward.
Two facts to internalise:
• It exists if and only if the graph is a DAG. A cyclea -> b -> a obviously cannot be linearised.
• It is usually not unique. 1 3 6 2 4 5 is also valid for G2. If a problem wants a specific one, it
will say “lexicographically smallest”, and that changes the algorithm slightly .
Undirected graphs do not have topological orders. This is a directed-only concept.
8.2 Kahn’s algorithm, the BFS way
The idea in one sentence: repeatedly output a vertex that has no remaining prerequisites.
compute indegree of every vertex
put all vertices with indegree 0 into a queue
while the queue is not empty:
pop u, append it to the order
for each edge u -> v:
indegree[v] -= 1 // u is done, one prerequisite less
if indegree[v] == 0: push v
if the order has fewer than n vertices: the graph has a cycle
50

--- Page Break ---

Topological Sort and DP on a DAG 51
vector<int> topoSort(int n, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
vector<int> indeg(n + 1, 0);
for (int u = 1; u <= n; u++)
for (int v : adj[u])
indeg[v]++;
queue<int> q;
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
if (indeg[i] == 0) q.push(i);
vector<int> order;
while (!q.empty()) {
int u = q.front(); q.pop();
order.push_back(u);
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.push(v);
}
}
if ((int)order.size() < n) return {}; // cycle: no topological order exists
return order;
}
8.2.1 Dry run on G2
indegrees: 1:0 2:1 3:1 4:2 5:2 6:1
queue starts with all indegree 0 vertices: q = [1]
pop 1 order = [1]
edge 1->2: indeg[2] 1->0, push
edge 1->3: indeg[3] 1->0, push q = [2,3]
pop 2 order = [1,2]
edge 2->4: indeg[4] 2->1 q = [3]
pop 3 order = [1,2,3]
edge 3->4: indeg[4] 1->0, push
edge 3->6: indeg[6] 1->0, push q = [4,6]
pop 4 order = [1,2,3,4]
edge 4->5: indeg[5] 2->1 q = [6]
pop 6 order = [1,2,3,4,6]
edge 6->5: indeg[5] 1->0, push q = [5]
pop 5 order = [1,2,3,4,6,5] q = []
6 vertices produced out of 6, so no cycle.
Check the result against every edge: 1->2 ok, 1->3 ok, 2->4 ok, 3->4 ok, 3->6 ok, 4->5 ok, 6->5 ok.

--- Page Break ---

Topological Sort and DP on a DAG 52
Every arrow points to the right.
Time O(n + m), space O(n).
8.2.2 Cycle detection, free of charge
If the graph has a cycle, the vertices on that cycle can never reach indegree 0, because each of them is
waiting for another one on the same cycle. So they never enter the queue and the output is short.
order.size() < n is a complete and correct cycle test for directed graphs, and it is iterative, so there
is no recursion depth risk.
This is often the easiest way to answer “is this directed graph acyclic”.
8.3 The DFS way
Run a DFS. When a vertex finishes (all of its descendants are done), push it to a list. Reverse the list
at the end.
vector<int> order;
vector<int> color; // 0 white, 1 grey, 2 black
bool dfs(int u, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
color[u] = 1;
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (color[v] == 1) return false ; // cycle
if (color[v] == 0 && !dfs(v, adj)) return false ;
}
color[u] = 2;
order.push_back(u); // postorder position
return true ;
}
// after running dfs from every white vertex:
reverse(order.begin(), order.end());
Why does reversed postorder work? A vertex finishes only after everything reachable from it has
finished. So in the postorder list, every descendant appears before its ancestor. Reverse it and every
ancestor comes first, which is exactly the topological condition.
This is the same postorder position you used for bottom-up work in the trees course. Same idea, new
use.
8.3.1 Dry run on G2
dfs(1) -> dfs(2) -> dfs(4) -> dfs(5), 5 has no outgoing, finish 5
finish 4
finish 2
-> dfs(3): 4 is black, skip
dfs(6): 5 is black, skip, finish 6
finish 3
finish 1

--- Page Break ---

Topological Sort and DP on a DAG 53
postorder : 5 4 2 6 3 1
reversed : 1 3 6 2 4 5
A different valid order from Kahn’s. Both are correct. If a checker expects one specific order, read the
statement again.
8.4 Lexicographically smallest topological order
Replace the queue with a min-heap. At every step, among all vertices currently available, take the
smallest.
priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>> pq;
// everything else is identical to Kahn
Time O(n + m log n).
This is a very common problem twist (“print the alphabetically first valid order”). Note that greedy is
correct here only because any available vertex can legally be taken now, so taking the smallest never
blocks anything.
Careful: this is not the same as “sort the topological order”. You may only choose among vertices
whose prerequisites are already satisfied.
8.5 DP on a DAG
This is where topological order earns its keep. A DAG has no cycles, so once you have a topological
order, you can do dynamic programming in that order and every dependency is already computed.
The pattern:
process vertices in topological order
for each edge u -> v: update dp[v] using dp[u]
8.5.1 Counting paths
How many distinct paths lead from vertex 1 to vertex 5 in G2?
vector<long long> cnt(n + 1, 0);
cnt[1] = 1;
for (int u : order)
for (int v : adj[u])
cnt[v] += cnt[u];
order: 1 2 3 4 6 5
cnt[1] = 1
from 1: cnt[2] = 1, cnt[3] = 1
from 2: cnt[4] = 1
from 3: cnt[4] = 2, cnt[6] = 1
from 4: cnt[5] = 2
from 6: cnt[5] = 3

--- Page Break ---

Topological Sort and DP on a DAG 54
answer: 3 paths, namely 1-2-4-5, 1-3-4-5, 1-3-6-5
Use long long, or take everything modulo whatever the problem says. Path counts explode.
8.5.2 Longest path in a DAG
In a general graph the longest path problem is NP-hard. In a DAG it is a four line DP, and this contrast
is worth remembering.
vector<int> dp(n + 1, 0); // longest path ending at v, in edges
for (int u : order)
for (int v : adj[u])
dp[v] = max(dp[v], dp[u] + 1);
int answer = *max_element(dp.begin() + 1, dp.end());
On G2, starting the count from vertex 1:
dp[1]=0
dp[2]=1 dp[3]=1
dp[4]=max(dp[2]+1, dp[3]+1)=2
dp[6]=dp[3]+1=2
dp[5]=max(dp[4]+1, dp[6]+1)=3
longest path has 3 edges: 1-2-4-5 or 1-3-6-5 or 1-3-4-5
With weights, replace +1 with +w. This also solves “longest increasing path in a grid” once you notice
the grid becomes a DAG when you only allow moves to strictly larger cells.
8.5.3 Other things this pattern solves
shortest path in a DAG, even with negative weights dp[v] = min(dp[v], dp[u] + w)
number of paths dp[v] += dp[u]
can vertex t be reached from s boolean dp
maximum profit picking a chain of tasks weighted longest path
course scheduling feasibility does a topological order exist
minimum number of semesters longest path plus one
Notice that a DAG with negative weights is easy , while a general graph with negative weights needs
Bellman-Ford. Cycles are what makes shortest paths hard, not negative numbers.
8.6 Common mistakes
• Running topological sort on an undirected graph. The concept does not apply .
• Counting indegree by looping over adj[v]. Indegree of v is the number of edges into v, so it is
incremented while scanning adj[u] for all u.
• Forgetting the order.size() < n check. Then a cyclic input silently produces a partial order.
• Using --indeg[v] == 0 incorrectly, for example writing indeg[v]-- == 0, which compares
before decrementing.
• Sorting the finished order to make it lexicographically smallest. Wrong. Use a priority queue
during the algorithm.

--- Page Break ---

Topological Sort and DP on a DAG 55
• Doing the DP without a topological order. The whole point is that the order guarantees
dependencies are ready .
• Overflow when counting paths.
8.7 Codeforces problems that test exactly this
• 510C, Fox And Names. Build a graph from letter constraints, then topologically sort. https:
//codeforces.com/problemset/problem/510/C
• 999E, Reachability from the Capital. Uses the DAG of components, see Part 13. https://codeforces
.com/problemset/problem/999/E
• 1100E, Andrew and Taxi. Binary search plus cycle detection on a directed graph. https://codeforc
es.com/problemset/problem/1100/E
8.8 Check yourself
1. When does a topological order exist?
2. Why does Kahn’s algorithm produce fewer than n vertices exactly when there is a cycle?
3. Why is reversed DFS postorder a valid topological order?
4. Give a second valid topological order of G2, different from both in the text.
5. How do you get the lexicographically smallest order, and why is the greedy choice safe?
6. Why is longest path easy on a DAG but hard in general?
7. How many paths are there from vertex 1 to vertex 4 in G2? Verify with the DP.

--- Page Break ---

section_based.text:
Part 9
Disjoint Set Union
The competitive programmer’s favourite data structure
9.1 The problem it solves
You have n items, initially all separate. Two operations arrive in any order, many times:
union(a, b) put a and b into the same group
find(a) which group is a in
and the real question is usually find(a) == find(b), meaning “are a and b in the same group”.
DFS answers connectivity once, in O(n + m). It cannot handle edges arriving over time, because
every new edge would need a fresh traversal. DSU handles both operations in essentially constant
time, which is why it appears in an enormous fraction of contest problems.
Other names for it: Union-Find, disjoint set forest.
9.2 The idea
Every group is a tree, and the root of that tree is the group’s name. find(x) walks up to the root.
union(a, b) hangs one root under the other.
initially after union(1,2) after union(1,4)
1 2 3 4 5 1 3 4 5 1 3 5
/ / \
2 2 4
The shape of these trees is meaningless. Only “who is the root” matters.
9.3 Version 1, the naive one
int parent[N];
void init(int n) { for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) parent[i] = i; }
int find(int x) {
while (parent[x] != x) x = parent[x];
return x;
56

--- Page Break ---

Disjoint Set Union 57
}
void unite(int a, int b) {
a = find(a); b = find(b);
if (a != b) parent[a] = b;
}
Correct, and potentially O(n) per operation. Union in a bad order builds a chain:
union(1,2), union(2,3), union(3,4), ... produces
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> ... -> n
and find(1) walks the entire chain.
Two independent improvements fix this. Use both.
9.4 Improvement 1: path compression
While walking up in find, point every visited node straight at the root. The next find on any of them
is then one step.
int find(int x) {
if (parent[x] == x) return x;
return parent[x] = find(parent[x]); // compress on the way back up
}
That single line,parent[x] = find(parent[x]), does the whole job. It is a postorder assignment:
recurse to the root first, then rewrite the pointer.
before find(4) after find(4)
1 1
| /|\
2 2 3 4
|
3
|
4
9.5 Improvement 2: union by size
Always hang the smaller tree under the larger one. Then no tree ever gets deep, because a tree only
gains depth when it is merged into something at least as big, which means the total size at least
doubles.
int parent[N], sz[N];
void init(int n) {

--- Page Break ---

Disjoint Set Union 58
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) { parent[i] = i; sz[i] = 1; }
}
int find(int x) {
if (parent[x] == x) return x;
return parent[x] = find(parent[x]);
}
bool unite(int a, int b) {
a = find(a); b = find(b);
if (a == b) return false ; // already together, nothing to do
if (sz[a] < sz[b]) swap(a, b); // a is now the bigger root
parent[b] = a;
sz[a] += sz[b];
return true ;
}
That is the whole structure. Twenty lines, and you should be able to type it from memory in ninety
seconds. unite returning a boolean is deliberate: false means “these were already connected”,
which is precisely the cycle test and precisely what Kruskal needs.
Union by rank (tree height) is an equivalent alternative. Size is more useful, because component sizes
are often part of the answer.
9.6 Complexity
With both improvements, m operations on n elements cost O(m alpha(n)), where alpha is the inverse
Ackermann function. For any n that fits in the universe, alpha(n) <= 4. So treat it as constant time
and write O(m) or O(n + m) in your analysis.
With only path compression, or only union by size, it is O(log n) per operation, which is also fine in
practice. With neither, it is O(n) per operation and it will fail.
Space O(n).
9.7 Dry run: G1 edge by edge
edges in input order: 1-2 1-4 2-3 2-4 2-5 3-6 4-5 7-8
start parent = [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8] sizes all 1
1-2 find(1)=1, find(2)=2, different
sizes equal, hang 2 under 1 parent[2]=1, sz[1]=2
1-4 find(1)=1, find(4)=4, different
sz[1]=2 > sz[4]=1, hang 4 under 1 parent[4]=1, sz[1]=3
2-3 find(2)=1, find(3)=3, different parent[3]=1, sz[1]=4
2-4 find(2)=1, find(4)=1, SAME -> this edge closes a cycle
2-5 find(2)=1, find(5)=5, different parent[5]=1, sz[1]=5
3-6 find(3)=1, find(6)=6, different parent[6]=1, sz[1]=6

--- Page Break ---

Disjoint Set Union 59
4-5 find(4)=1, find(5)=1, SAME -> cycle again
7-8 different parent[8]=7, sz[7]=2
final groups: {1,2,3,4,5,6} with root 1, {7,8} with root 7
edges that closed a cycle: 2
Cross-check with the formula from Part 6: m - (n - c) = 8 - (8 - 2) = 2. The two counts agree,
as they must.
9.8 What DSU is used for
connectivity queries, online find(a) == find(b)
counting components start at n, decrement on every successful unite
component sizes sz[find(v)]
cycle detection while adding edges unite returns false
Kruskal's MST Part 10
grouping equal or equivalent items "these two are the same", transitively
grid connectivity id = x * C + y
offline queries in reverse process deletions backwards as insertions
9.8.1 Counting components with DSU
int comps = n;
// each time unite() actually merges:
if (unite(a, b)) comps--;
Starting from n singletons, every successful merge reduces the count by exactly one. This is the
standard answer to “after each new road, how many separate regions remain”.
9.8.2 The reverse trick
DSU can merge but cannot split. When a problem deletes edges or vertices over time, read all the
queries first and process them backwards, so deletions become additions. This is a genuinely common
technique and worth remembering as a shape, even before you meet a problem that needs it.
9.9 Common mistakes
• Comparing parent[a] == parent[b] instead of find(a) == find(b) . Parents are not roots.
This is the number one DSU bug.
• Uniting without calling find first. parent[a] = b where a is not a root corrupts the structure.
• Forgetting init, or initialising parent[i] = 0 instead of i.
• Sizing the arrays n instead of n + 1 with 1-indexed vertices.
• Not resetting between test cases.
• Using DSU on a directed graph expecting it to respect directions. It cannot. DSU only knows
undirected connectivity .
• Recursion depth in find. With path compression the trees stay shallow, so this is safe in practice,
but if you skip union by size the recursion can be deep on adversarial input.
• Expecting DSU to support splitting. It does not.

--- Page Break ---

Disjoint Set Union 60
9.10 Codeforces problems that test exactly this
• 217A, Ice Skating. https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/217/A
• 445B, DZY Loves Chemistry . https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/445/B
• 25D, Roads not only in Berland. Count redundant edges, reconnect components. https://codeforc
es.com/problemset/problem/25/D
• 455C, Civilization. DSU plus tree diameters. A very good exercise once you finish Part 12.
https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/455/C
• 500B, New Year Permutation. Positions that can be swapped form groups. https://codeforces.com
/problemset/problem/500/B
9.11 Check yourself
1. Why is parent[a] == parent[b] the wrong test?
2. What are the two optimisations, and what does each one prevent?
3. Explain the line return parent[x] = find(parent[x]); in words.
4. What does it mean when unite(a, b) returns false, and which algorithm uses that?
5. Starting from n singletons, how do you maintain the number of components?
6. Why can DSU not undo a union, and what is the standard workaround?
7. G1 processed edge by edge produced two “already connected” events. Predict that number from n,
m and the component count.

--- Page Break ---

Part 10
Minimum Spanning Tree
Kruskal and Prim
10.1 The problem
Given a connected undirected weighted graph, choose a subset of edges that
1. keeps everything connected, and
2. has the smallest possible total weight.
Such a subset is always a tree on all n vertices: it has exactly n - 1 edges and no cycles. If it had a
cycle you could delete an edge of that cycle and stay connected while paying less. Hence the name
minimum spanning tree, MST.
Typical phrasing in problems: connect all cities with roads at minimum cost; lay cable so every house
has power; make the network connected as cheaply as possible.
If the graph is disconnected there is no spanning tree. Then the answer is usually a minimum
spanning forest, one tree per component, and the problem will say so or will guarantee connectivity .
10.2 The working example, G3
edges (undirected, weighted):
1-2 : 7 1-3 : 9 1-6 : 14
2-3 : 10 2-4 : 15
3-4 : 11 3-6 : 2
4-5 : 6 5-6 : 9
n = 6, m = 9
The MST we are aiming for:
3-6 (2), 4-5 (6), 1-2 (7), 1-3 (9), 5-6 (9) 5 edges, total 33
10.3 The one idea behind both algorithms
The cut property. Split the vertices into any two non-empty groups. Look at all edges crossing
between the groups. The cheapest one of those can always be part of some MST.
61

--- Page Break ---

Minimum Spanning Tree 62
The intuition: the two groups must be joined somehow, so at least one crossing edge is in the tree. If
your tree uses a more expensive crossing edge, swap it for the cheapest one. You stay connected and
pay less.
Kruskal applies this globally by weight order. Prim applies it locally around a growing blob. That is
the only real difference between them.
10.4 Kruskal’s algorithm
sort all edges by weight, ascending
for each edge (u, v, w) in that order:
if u and v are in different components:
take the edge
union their components
stop when you have n - 1 edges
The “different components” test is exactly unite() from Part 9, which is why Kruskal is taught right
after DSU.
struct Edge {
int u, v, w;
bool operator<(const Edge& o) const { return w < o.w; }
};
long long kruskal(int n, vector<Edge>& edges) {
sort(edges.begin(), edges.end());
init(n); // DSU init
long long total = 0;
int used = 0;
for (const Edge& e : edges) {
if (unite(e.u, e.v)) { // false means it would make a cycle
total += e.w;
used++;
if (used == n - 1) break;
}
}
if (used < n - 1) return -1; // graph was disconnected
return total;
}
To output the edges themselves, pushe into a vector inside the if.
10.4.1 Dry run on G3
sorted edges:
3-6 (2) 4-5 (6) 1-2 (7) 1-3 (9) 5-6 (9)
2-3 (10) 3-4 (11) 1-6 (14) 2-4 (15)
3-6 (2) different -> take. groups: {3,6} {1} {2} {4} {5} total 2

--- Page Break ---

Minimum Spanning Tree 63
4-5 (6) different -> take. groups: {3,6} {4,5} {1} {2} total 8
1-2 (7) different -> take. groups: {1,2} {3,6} {4,5} total 15
1-3 (9) different -> take. groups: {1,2,3,6} {4,5} total 24
5-6 (9) different -> take. groups: {1,2,3,4,5,6} total 33
5 edges = n - 1, stop
MST = { 3-6, 4-5, 1-2, 1-3, 5-6 }, weight 33
Notice that 2-3 (10), 3-4 (11), 1-6 (14) and 2-4 (15) were never even examined, because we
stopped early . Also notice we would have rejected2-3 anyway: by then 2 and 3 were already in the
same group.
Time O(m log m) for the sort, plus O(m alpha(n)) for the DSU, so O(m log m) overall. Since m <=
nˆ2, log m <= 2 log n, and you will also see this written as O(m log n). Space O(n + m).
10.5 Prim’s algorithm
Grow one tree from a starting vertex. Repeatedly add the cheapest edge that leaves the current tree.
put vertex 1 in the tree
repeat n - 1 times:
among all edges from the tree to outside, take the cheapest
add its outside endpoint to the tree
To find “the cheapest edge leaving the tree” quickly , keep a priority queue of candidate edges.
long long prim(int n, vector<vector<pair<int,int>>>& adj) {
vector<bool> inTree(n + 1, false);
priority_queue<pair<int,int>, vector<pair<int,int>>,
greater<pair<int,int>>> pq; // (weight, vertex)
long long total = 0;
int taken = 0;
pq.push({0, 1}); // start at vertex 1, cost 0
while (!pq.empty() && taken < n) {
auto [w, u] = pq.top(); pq.pop();
if (inTree[u]) continue; // stale entry, skip
inTree[u] = true;
total += w;
taken++;
for (auto [v, wt] : adj[u])
if (!inTree[v])
pq.push({wt, v});
}
if (taken < n) return -1; // disconnected
return total;
}

--- Page Break ---

Minimum Spanning Tree 64
Note the pair is (weight, vertex), because the priority queue sorts by the first element. This is
the opposite order from the adjacency list, which stores (neighbour, weight). Mixing them up is a
classic bug, so read your own code once before submitting.
10.5.1 Dry run on G3
start: tree = {1}, total = 0
candidates from 1: (7,2) (9,3) (14,6)
take (7,2) tree={1,2} total=7
add (10,3) (15,4)
candidates: (9,3) (10,3) (14,6) (15,4)
take (9,3) tree={1,2,3} total=16
add (11,4) (2,6)
candidates: (2,6) (10,3 stale) (11,4) (14,6) (15,4)
take (2,6) tree={1,2,3,6} total=18
add (9,5)
candidates: (9,5) (11,4) (14,6 stale) (15,4)
take (9,5) tree={1,2,3,5,6} total=27
add (6,4)
candidates: (6,4) (11,4) (15,4)
take (6,4) tree=all total=33
MST = { 1-2, 1-3, 3-6, 5-6, 4-5 }, weight 33
Same weight, same edge set as Kruskal. That is not luck: when all edge weights are distinct, the MST
is unique. With ties, different algorithms may produce different trees of equal weight.
Time O(m log n) with a binary heap. Space O(n + m).
10.5.2 The dense version of Prim
If the graph is dense and given as a matrix, skip the heap: keep an array minEdge[v] and each round
scan all vertices for the smallest. That is O(n2), which beats O(m log n) when m is near n2.
// O(nˆ2) Prim, for n <= about 5000 with an adjacency matrix
vector<int> minE(n + 1, INF);
vector<bool> used(n + 1, false);
minE[1] = 0;
long long total = 0;
for (int it = 0; it < n; it++) {
int u = -1;
for (int v = 1; v <= n; v++)
if (!used[v] && (u == -1 || minE[v] < minE[u])) u = v;
if (minE[u] == INF) return -1; // disconnected
used[u] = true;
total += minE[u];

--- Page Break ---

Minimum Spanning Tree 65
for (int v = 1; v <= n; v++)
if (!used[v]) minE[v] = min(minE[v], g[u][v]);
}
This version appears in problems where the graph is complete and the weight is a formula, for example
“the cost between two points is their Manhattan distance”. Building all n 2 edges for Kruskal would be
too slow; O(n2) Prim is exactly right. Codeforces 1245D is the standard example.
10.6 Kruskal or Prim
Kruskal Prim (heap) Prim (n 2)
Complexity O(m log m) O(m log n) O(n 2)
Best when sparse, edge list given sparse, adjacency list
given
dense, or complete
graphs
Needs DSU, sorted edges priority queue matrix
Handles disconnected
input
yes, gives a forest no, only reaches one
component
no
Easier to write usually yes close yes
Default to Kruskal. Switch to O(n2) Prim when the graph is complete or nearly so.
10.7 Useful variants
• Maximum spanning tree: sort descending, or negate the weights. Everything else is unchanged.
• Minimum spanning forest: run Kruskal and do not require n - 1 edges. The result has n - c
edges.
• Some edges are forced: union them first, then run Kruskal on the rest.
• Is the MST unique? It is unique if, at every step, the choice was forced. A practical test: for
each edge not in the MST, check whether it ties with the maximum edge weight on the tree path
between its endpoints.
• A virtual vertex: problems like “you may either build a power plant in city i for cost c[i], or lay a
cable between cities” become a plain MST if you add a vertex 0 joined to city i with weight c[i].
Then a spanning tree of the enlarged graph is exactly a valid plan. This trick is worth memorising,
it shows up regularly .
10.8 Common mistakes
• Forgetting to sort the edges.
• Using find results incorrectly, that is, uniting non-roots.
• Not detecting disconnection. Check the edge count or the vertex count at the end.
• Overflow. With m up to 2 * 105 and weights up to 109, the total needs long long.
• Mixing (w, v) and (v, w) orders in Prim.
• Forgetting the stale-entry check if (inTree[u]) continue; in heap Prim.

--- Page Break ---

Minimum Spanning Tree 66
• Believing the MST minimises the distance between two specific vertices. It does not. The path
between two vertices in an MST is a minimax path (its largest edge is as small as possible), not a
shortest path. Confusing MST with shortest paths is a real conceptual error.
10.9 Codeforces problems that test exactly this
• 1245D, Shichikuji and Power Grid. The virtual vertex trick, plus O(n2) Prim. https://codeforces.c
om/problemset/problem/1245/D
• 76A, Gift. MST with two weight functions. https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/76/A
• 25D, Roads not only in Berland. Reuse redundant edges to connect components. https://codeforc
es.com/problemset/problem/25/D
• 1108F, MST Unification. Counting when an edge can be replaced. https://codeforces.com/probl
emset/problem/1108/F
10.10 Check yourself
1. Why does an MST always have exactly n - 1 edges?
2. State the cut property , and say how Kruskal and Prim each use it.
3. On G3, why was the edge 2-3 (10) rejected by Kruskal?
4. When is the MST guaranteed unique?
5. Which Prim variant do you use on a complete graph with n = 2000, and why?
6. How do you compute a maximum spanning tree with the same code?
7. Is the path between u and v in the MST the shortest path between them? Justify your answer.

--- Page Break ---

Part 11
Shortest Paths
BFS, 0-1 BFS, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall
11.1 Choosing the algorithm
Do this before writing a single line. The choice is decided by the weights, not by the problem’s story .
Situation Algorithm Complexity
All edges weight 1 (or
unweighted)
BFS O(n + m)
All weights are 0 or 1 0-1 BFS with a deque O(n + m)
Weights small, say 0 to k dial’s buckets, or Dijkstra O(n + m) k, or O(m log n)
Weights non-negative Dijkstra O(m log n)
Some weights negative Bellman-Ford O(n m)
Need distances between all
pairs, n small
Floyd-Warshall O(n 3)
The graph is a DAG topological order DP (Part 8) O(n + m)
Two sentences worth memorising:
• Negative weights break Dijkstra. Not “make it slow”, break it.
• Negative cycles make the question meaningless, because you can loop forever and pay less each
time. Bellman-Ford and Floyd can both detect them.
11.2 1. Unweighted: BFS
Covered in Part 4. One queue, dist[v] = dist[u] + 1, set at push time. O(n + m). If every edge
costs the same amount c, run BFS and multiply by c at the end.
11.3 2. Weights 0 and 1: 0-1 BFS
Suppose every edge costs 0 or 1. Dijkstra would work but carries a log factor. There is a better way .
Idea: keep the queue sorted by distance without a heap. When you relax an edge of weight 0, the
new vertex has the same distance as the current one, so it belongs at the front. When the edge has
weight 1, it belongs at the back. A deque does both in O(1).
67

--- Page Break ---

Shortest Paths 68
vector<int> zeroOneBfs(int s, int n, vector<vector<pair<int,int>>>& adj) {
vector<int> d(n + 1, INT_MAX);
deque<int> dq;
d[s] = 0;
dq.push_front(s);
while (!dq.empty()) {
int u = dq.front(); dq.pop_front();
for (auto [v, w] : adj[u]) {
if (d[u] + w < d[v]) {
d[v] = d[u] + w;
if (w == 0) dq.push_front(v);
else dq.push_back(v);
}
}
}
return d;
}
The deque always holds at most two distinct distance values, k and k + 1, with all the ks in front.

11.4 3. Non-negative weights: Dijkstra
11.4.1 The idea
Keep a set of vertices whose distance is already final. Repeatedly take the unfinished vertex with the
smallest tentative distance, declare it final, and relax its outgoing edges.
Why is the smallest tentative distance final? Because all weights are non-negative, so any other route
to it would have to pass through some unfinished vertex first, which already has a larger tentative
distance, and adding non-negative weights cannot make it smaller. That argument fails the moment
a weight is negative, which is why Dijkstra requires non-negative weights.
11.4.2 The code
const long long INF = 1e18;
vector<long long> dijkstra(int s, int n, vector<vector<pair<int,int>>>& adj) {
vector<long long> d(n + 1, INF);
priority_queue<pair<long long,int>,
vector<pair<long long,int>>,
greater<pair<long long,int>>> pq; // min-heap of (dist, vertex)
d[s] = 0;
pq.push({0, s});
while (!pq.empty()) {
auto [du, u] = pq.top(); pq.pop();
if (du > d[u]) continue; // stale entry, we already did better
for (auto [v, w] : adj[u]) {
if (d[u] + w < d[v]) {
d[v] = d[u] + w;
pq.push({d[v], v}); // lazy: push a new entry, never update in place
}
}
}
return d;
}
Three details that matter:
• (dist, vertex) order in the heap, because pairs compare on the first element.
• The stale check if (du > d[u]) continue;. We never remove outdated entries, we just ignore
them. Without this line the algorithm still gives correct answers but does far more work.
• long long for distances. With 105 edges of weight 109, a path can reach 1014. This is the single
most common Dijkstra bug in contests.
Time O(m log n), because each edge can push at most one heap entry and each heap operation is
O(log). Space O(n + m).

• Multi-source: push every source with distance 0, exactly as in BFS.
• Dijkstra on a grid: the neighbour loop changes, nothing else. Common when moving into a cell

• Virtual vertex: “you may start at any of these k cities” becomes one source vertex joined to those
k with weight 0.
• State expansion: when the answer depends on more than the vertex, make the state bigger.
d[v][k] for “at v having used k free tickets” is still Dijkstra, on a graph with n * (k+1) vertices.
This is the single most useful advanced idea in this part, and Part 14 returns to it.
• Counting shortest paths: keep cnt[v]. When you improve d[v], set cnt[v] = cnt[u]. When
you tie, do cnt[v] += cnt[u].
11.5 4. Negative weights: Bellman-Ford
11.5.1 The idea
A shortest path has at most n - 1 edges (any more and it repeats a vertex, so it contains a cycle,
which we may drop). So: relax every edge, n - 1 times. After round i, all shortest paths using at
most i edges are correct.
struct Edge { int u, v, w; };
vector<long long> bellmanFord(int s, int n, vector<Edge>& edges, bool& hasNegCycle) {
vector<long long> d(n + 1, INF);
d[s] = 0;
for (int i = 0; i < n - 1; i++) {
bool changed = false;
for (const Edge& e : edges) {
if (d[e.u] < INF && d[e.u] + e.w < d[e.v]) {
d[e.v] = d[e.u] + e.w;
changed = true;
}
}
if (!changed) break; // early exit, common and worth having
}
hasNegCycle = false;

if (d[e.u] < INF && d[e.u] + e.w < d[e.v])

11.5.3 Detecting a negative cycle
If any edge can still be relaxed after n - 1 rounds, some path is getting shorter forever, which means
a negative cycle is reachable from the source. To find which vertices are affected, run one more
round and mark every vertex you improve, then propagate that mark along all outgoing edges with a
BFS or DFS.
Time O(n m). Space O(n + m).
That complexity is why Bellman-Ford is the last resort. With n and m both 105 it is 1010 operations and
hopeless. It is used when n is small, or when negative weights genuinely appear (currency arbitrage,
profit and cost mixed together).
SPFA is a queue-based optimisation of Bellman-Ford that is usually fast but has a worst case of O(n
m), and Codeforces problem setters have written anti-SPFA tests. Know it exists; do not rely on it.

11.8 Common mistakes
• Using int for distances. Sums overflow. Uselong long unless you have checked.
• Setting INF = INT_MAX and then adding to it. Overflow to negative. Use 1e18 with long long,
or 1e9 with int and guard before adding.
• Using BFS on a weighted graph.
• Using Dijkstra with negative weights.
• Omitting the stale check in Dijkstra.
• Putting k in the wrong loop position in Floyd.
• Forgetting d[i][i] = 0 when initialising Floyd’s matrix.
• Forgetting the unreachable case in the output.
• Forgetting that the graph may be directed and adding both directions anyway .
• Relaxing INF vertices in Bellman-Ford.
• Using priority_queue as a max-heap by accident. The default is a max-heap; you need
greater<> for a min-heap, or push negative distances.

12.4 Subtree DP
Anything of the form “for every vertex, compute something about its subtree” is this same DFS with a
different accumulation line:
subtree size sz[u] += sz[v]
subtree sum of values sum[u] += sum[v]
number of leaves if u has no child, 1, else the sum over children
max value in subtree best[u] = max(best[u], best[v])
count of white nodes cnt[u] += cnt[v], plus 1 if u is white
depth of subtree h[u] = max(h[u], h[v] + 1)
Codeforces 161D (“Distance in Tree”, count pairs at distance exactly k) is a good first non-trivial
subtree DP, and 1092F is a good first rerooting problem, where you compute an answer for every
possible root in O(n) total.

12.5 Tree diameter
The diameter is the number of edges on the longest path between any two vertices. In our tree it is 6,
along 7 - 5 - 2 - 1 - 3 - 6 - 9.
12.5.1 Method 1: two BFS runs
1. BFS from any vertex, find the farthest vertex a.
2. BFS from a, find the farthest vertex b.
3. dist(a, b) is the diameter.
pair<int,int> bfsFar(int s, int n, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
vector<int> d(n + 1, -1);
queue<int> q; d[s] = 0; q.push(s);
int best = s;
while (!q.empty()) {
int u = q.front(); q.pop();
if (d[u] > d[best]) best = u;
for (int v : adj[u]) if (d[v] == -1) { d[v] = d[u] + 1; q.push(v); }
}
return {best, d[best]}; // farthest vertex and its distance
}
int diameter(int n, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
int a = bfsFar(1, n, adj).first;
return bfsFar(a, n, adj).second;
}
Why does it work? Because the farthest vertex from any starting vertex is always an endpoint of
some diameter. Sketch: let the diameter be a..b. If the search from s ended at some x that is not an
endpoint, you could splice the paths..x into the diameter and get something longer, contradiction.
The full proof is a short case analysis and worth reading once.

12.6 LCA and distances
The lowest common ancestor of u and v, once the tree is rooted, is the deepest vertex that is an
ancestor of both. In our tree, LCA(4, 8) = 2 and LCA(7, 9) = 1.
The reason it matters:
dist(u, v) = dep[u] + dep[v] - 2 * dep[LCA(u, v)]
Check: dist(4, 8) = 2 + 3 - 2 * dep[2] = 2 + 3 - 2 = 3, and indeed the path is 4 - 2 - 5
- 8.
Once you can compute LCA in O(log n), you can answer path queries between arbitrary vertices,
which is the workhorse of tree problems.

up[v][0] = parent of v
up[v][k] = up[ up[v][k-1] ][k-1] two jumps of 2^(k-1) make one of 2^k

for (int v : adj[u])
if (v != p) { dep[v] = dep[u] + 1; dfs(v, u, adj); }
}
int lca(int u, int v) {
if (dep[u] < dep[v]) swap(u, v);
int diff = dep[u] - dep[v];
for (int k = 0; k < LOG; k++) // lift u to v's depth
if (diff >> k & 1) u = up[u][k];

• Forgetting if (v == p) continue; and recursing back and forth forever.

there.

• Assuming the tree is rooted at 1 when the problem roots it elsewhere. Read the statement.
• LOG too small. With n = 2 * 105 you need at least 18.
• Not handling up[root][k]. Point it at a sentinel, usually 0.
• Recursion depth on a path-shaped tree with n = 10 5. This is the standard shape of an
anti-recursion test.
• Recomputing depth with a separate traversal when the same DFS could have done it.

3. Give the subtree sizes of every vertex in the example tree, and check them against n.
4. State the two-BFS diameter method and the reason it works.
5. Compute dist(7, 9) using depths and the LCA.
6. In binary lifting, why do we move only when up[u][k] != up[v][k]?
7. What does tin and tout buy you that a plain DFS does not?
8. Your LCA answers are wrong for deep vertices only . What is the first thing you check?

--- Page Break ---

Part 13
The DFS Tree, Bridges and Strong Connectivity
Advanced, but very much learnable
This part is marked advanced. Everything in it is one idea applied three times: the DFS tree tells you
which vertices can reach back upward, and that answers questions about what happens when
you remove things. Do not skip it out of fear. Do skip it if you have not yet solved twenty problems
from the earlier parts.
13.1 Recap: the DFS tree
Run a DFS on an undirected graph. Tree edges are the ones DFS walks along. Every other edge is a
back edge, joining a vertex to one of its own ancestors. There are no sideways edges (Part 3 explains
why).
Working example for this part:
1 --- 2
\ /
3
|
4
/ \
5 --- 6
edges: 1-2 2-3 1-3 3-4 4-5 5-6 4-6
Two triangles joined by a single edge3-4. Intuitively , that edge is the weak point: cut it and the graph
falls apart. Vertices 3 and 4 are also weak: delete either one and the graph falls apart. We want to
find such edges and vertices automatically .
13.2 tin and low
Two numbers per vertex:
• tin[v]: the time at which DFS first entered v.
• low[v]: the smallest tin reachable from the subtree of v using tree edges downward and at most
one back edge.
In words: low[v] answers “how high up can the subtree of v climb without using the edge to its
parent?”
82

--- Page Break ---

The DFS Tree, Bridges and Strong Connectivity 83
int timer = 0;
vector<int> tin, low;
vector<bool> vis;
void dfs(int u, int p, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
vis[u] = true;
tin[u] = low[u] = timer++;
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (v == p) continue; // skip the edge to the parent
if (vis[v]) {
low[u] = min(low[u], tin[v]); // back edge: climb to v
} else {
dfs(v, u, adj);
low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]); // child's reach becomes mine
}
}
}
Note carefully: for a back edge we take tin[v], for a tree edge we takelow[v]. Mixing these up is
the standard bug, and it still gives correct answers on many small tests, which makes it hard to catch.
13.2.1 Dry run
dfs(1, 0): tin[1] = low[1] = 0
dfs(2, 1): tin[2] = low[2] = 1
dfs(3, 2): tin[3] = low[3] = 2
neighbour 1 is visited and is not the parent -> back edge, low[3] = min(2, tin[1]=0) = 0
dfs(4, 3): tin[4] = low[4] = 3
dfs(5, 4): tin[5] = low[5] = 4
dfs(6, 5): tin[6] = low[6] = 5
neighbour 4 is visited, not the parent -> low[6] = min(5, tin[4]=3) = 3
back in 5: low[5] = min(4, low[6]=3) = 3
back in 4: low[4] = min(3, low[5]=3) = 3
back in 3: low[3] = min(0, low[4]=3) = 0
back in 2: low[2] = min(1, low[3]=0) = 0
back in 1: low[1] = min(0, low[2]=0) = 0
vertex : 1 2 3 4 5 6
tin : 0 1 2 3 4 5
low : 0 0 0 3 3 3
13.3 Bridges
A bridge is an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components. Also called a cut
edge.
The tree edge u - v (with v a child of u) is a bridge if and only if low[v] > tin[u].
Read it as: the subtree of v cannot reach u or anything above u except through this edge. So cutting it

--- Page Break ---

The DFS Tree, Bridges and Strong Connectivity 84
isolates that subtree.
A back edge is never a bridge, because the cycle it closes provides an alternative route.
vector<pair<int,int>> bridges;
void dfs(int u, int p, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
vis[u] = true;
tin[u] = low[u] = timer++;
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (v == p) continue;
if (vis[v]) {
low[u] = min(low[u], tin[v]);
} else {
dfs(v, u, adj);
low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]);
if (low[v] > tin[u]) bridges.push_back({u, v});
}
}
}
On our example:
edge 1-2 : low[2]=0 > tin[1]=0 ? no
edge 2-3 : low[3]=0 > tin[2]=1 ? no
edge 3-4 : low[4]=3 > tin[3]=2 ? YES, bridge
edge 4-5 : low[5]=3 > tin[4]=3 ? no
edge 5-6 : low[6]=3 > tin[5]=4 ? no
the only bridge is 3-4, exactly as the picture suggested
Time O(n + m), space O(n).
Multiple edges caveat: if (v == p) continue; skips all edges to the parent, so a double edge
between u and v is wrongly treated as a single one, and the algorithm reports a bridge that is not one.
If the input may have multi-edges, skip by edge id instead of by vertex.
13.4 Articulation points
An articulation point (cut vertex) is a vertex whose removal increases the number of components.
Two rules, because the root of the DFS is special:
• For a non-root vertex u: it is an articulation point if it has a child v with low[v] >= tin[u]. Note
>=, not >. The subtree of v cannot get above u, so removing u cuts it off.
• For the root: it is an articulation point if and only if it has more than one child in the DFS tree.
With two or more children, the root is the only thing joining them.
set<int> aps;
void dfs(int u, int p, vector<vector<int>>& adj) {
vis[u] = true;

--- Page Break ---

The DFS Tree, Bridges and Strong Connectivity 85
tin[u] = low[u] = timer++;
int children = 0;
for (int v : adj[u]) {
if (v == p) continue;
if (vis[v]) {
low[u] = min(low[u], tin[v]);
} else {
dfs(v, u, adj);
low[u] = min(low[u], low[v]);
if (low[v] >= tin[u] && p != 0) aps.insert(u); // non-root rule
children++;
}
}
if (p == 0 && children > 1) aps.insert(u); // root rule
}
On our example:
vertex 1 is the root, children in the DFS tree: just {2} -> not an AP
vertex 2: child 3, low[3]=0 >= tin[2]=1 ? no -> not an AP
vertex 3: child 4, low[4]=3 >= tin[3]=2 ? YES -> AP
vertex 4: child 5, low[5]=3 >= tin[4]=3 ? YES -> AP
vertex 5: child 6, low[6]=3 >= tin[5]=4 ? no -> not an AP
vertex 6: no children -> not an AP
articulation points: 3 and 4
Which matches the picture: deleting 3 separates {1,2} from the rest, deleting 4 separates {5,6}.
Why >= here and > for bridges? For a bridge we need the subtree to be unable to reachu at all. For
an articulation point it is enough that the subtree cannot get strictly above u, because u itself is being
deleted.
13.5 Strongly connected components
Now directed graphs. In a directed graph, “connected” splits in two:
• Weakly connected: connected if you ignore the directions.
• Strongly connected: every vertex can reach every other vertex, following the directions.
A strongly connected component (SCC) is a maximal set of vertices that can all reach each other.
1 --> 2 --> 3 --> 4 --> 5 --> 7
^ | ^ |
| | | v
+-----------+ +---- 6
edges: 1->2 2->3 3->1 3->4 4->5 5->6 6->4 5->7
SCCs: {1,2,3} {4,5,6} {7}

--- Page Break ---

The DFS Tree, Bridges and Strong Connectivity 86
13.5.1 Kosaraju’s algorithm
Two DFS passes, and it is the easiest SCC algorithm to remember.
1. Run DFS on the graph. Push each vertex onto a list when it FINISHES.
2. Reverse every edge.
3. Process vertices in reverse finish order. Each DFS on the reversed graph
that starts from an unvisited vertex marks exactly one SCC.
vector<vector<int>> adj, radj;
vector<bool> vis;
vector<int> order, comp;
void dfs1(int u) {
vis[u] = true;
for (int v : adj[u]) if (!vis[v]) dfs1(v);
order.push_back(u); // finish time order
}
void dfs2(int u, int c) {
comp[u] = c;
for (int v : radj[u]) if (comp[v] == -1) dfs2(v, c);
}
int kosaraju(int n) {
vis.assign(n + 1, false);
order.clear();
for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) if (!vis[i]) dfs1(i);
comp.assign(n + 1, -1);
int c = 0;
for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) { // reverse finish order
int u = order[i];
if (comp[u] == -1) dfs2(u, c++);
}
return c; // number of SCCs
}
Build radj while reading the input: for every edge u -> v, push v into adj[u] and u into radj[v].
Why does it work? Intuition rather than proof: the vertex that finishes last in the first pass lies in a
“source” SCC of the condensation, one with no incoming edges from other components. Starting a
DFS from it in the reversed graph can only reach vertices of its own SCC, because the reversed edges
to other components point away . Peel that component off and repeat.
Time O(n + m), space O(n + m).
Tarjan’s algorithm does the same in a single pass usinglow values, similar in spirit to bridges. It is
faster by a constant factor and harder to recall under pressure. Learn Kosaraju first.
13.5.2 The condensation graph
Shrink each SCC to a single vertex. The result is always a DAG, because any cycle among components
would merge them into one component.
condensation of the example:

--- Page Break ---

The DFS Tree, Bridges and Strong Connectivity 87
[1,2,3] ---> [4,5,6] ---> [7]
This is enormously useful. Any question on a directed graph that is hard because of cycles becomes a
DAG question, and DAGs support topological sorting and DP (Part 8).
Typical uses:
• “How many extra edges to make the whole graph strongly connected?” Build the condensation,
count components with indegree 0 (call ita) and outdegree 0 (call itb). The answer is max(a, b),
or 0 if there is only one component.
• “From how few vertices can we reach everything?” Count the condensation components with
indegree 0. That is Codeforces 999E almost exactly .
• Longest path in a directed graph with cycles: condense, then DP on the DAG.
// building the condensation
for (int u = 1; u <= n; u++)
for (int v : adj[u])
if (comp[u] != comp[v])
cadj[comp[u]].push_back(comp[v]); // deduplicate if needed
13.6 Common mistakes
• Using low[v] instead of tin[v] on a back edge. The classic.
• Using > instead of >= for articulation points, or the reverse for bridges.
• Forgetting the special rule for the root.
• Skipping the parent by vertex when multi-edges exist. Skip by edge index.
• Forgetting to run the outer loop over all vertices on a disconnected graph.
• Building the reversed graph incorrectly in Kosaraju, most often by reversing only some edges.
• Assuming the condensation might have a cycle. It cannot.
• Recursion depth. These are all DFS, so a 2 * 105 chain is a real risk.
13.7 Codeforces problems that test exactly this
• 118E, Bertown roads. Orient every edge so the graph stays strongly connected. Possible exactly
when there is no bridge. https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/118/E
• 1000E, We Need More Bosses. Bridges, condensation into a tree, then tree diameter. A perfect
combination of Parts 12 and 13. https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1000/E
• 427C, Checkposts. SCCs, and count the cheapest vertex in each. https://codeforces.com/problem
set/problem/427/C
• 999E, Reachability from the Capital. Condensation and indegree-zero counting. https://codeforc
es.com/problemset/problem/999/E
13.8 Check yourself
1. Define low[v] in one sentence.

--- Page Break ---

The DFS Tree, Bridges and Strong Connectivity 88
2. Why do we use tin[v] for a back edge and low[v] for a tree edge?
3. Why is a back edge never a bridge?
4. State the bridge condition and the articulation point condition, and explain the difference between
> and >=.
5. Why does the root need its own rule?
6. What is the difference between weakly and strongly connected?
7. Why is the condensation always a DAG?
8. A directed graph has SCC condensation with 5 components, 2 of indegree 0 and 3 of outdegree 0.
How many edges must be added to make it strongly connected?

--- Page Break ---

metadata.section_title: Part 13 - The DFS Tree, Bridges and Strong Connectivity

section_based.text:
Part 14
How to Think About Graph Problems
Modelling first, algorithm second
This is the most important part of the course. Everything before it was equipment.
In a contest, the hard part is almost never “implement Dijkstra”. You can do that. The hard part is
noticing that the problem is a shortest path problem, and working out what the vertices are.
14.1 The ten questions
Ask these in order, on any problem that smells like a graph.
1. What are the vertices? Cities, cells, people, states of a process, positions plus extra information.
Write it down explicitly . If you cannot name the vertex set in one sentence, you have not modelled the
problem yet.
2. What are the edges, and what does one edge mean? “An edge means I can move from A to B in
one step.” One step of what?
3. Directed or undirected? Look for the word “one-way”, or an asymmetric relation. When in doubt,
ask whether the relation is symmetric.
4. Weighted or unweighted? Are all moves equally expensive? If yes, BFS. If the costs are 0 and 1,
deque. Otherwise Dijkstra.
5. Are there cycles? If the relation is “must happen before”, the graph should be a DAG, and a cycle
means the answer is “impossible”. That is often the entire problem.
6. What is being asked: reachability, distance, ordering, connectivity, or structure?
reachability -> DFS or BFS
distance -> BFS, 0-1 BFS, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd
ordering -> topological sort
connectivity -> components, DSU
structure -> bridges, articulation points, SCC, MST
7. How big is the graph? n and m decide whether O(n3), O(m log n) or O(n + m) is allowed. And if
the vertices are states, count the states before you build anything.
8. Is the graph explicit or implicit? An explicit graph is given as an edge list. An implicit graph
(grid, states, i -> a[i]) is generated on demand. Most of the hard modelling problems are implicit.
9. Does the state need more than the vertex? “Shortest path, but you may make up to k edges free”
is not a graph on n vertices. It is a graph on n * (k+1) states. This is the single most valuable idea in
this part.
89

--- Page Break ---

How to Think About Graph Problems 90
10. Is there a transformation that makes the problem standard? Reverse the edges. Add a super
source. Split a vertex into two. Take the complement. Condense the SCCs. Each of these turns a
strange problem into a textbook one.
14.2 The modelling catalogue
14.2.1 1. Explicit graph
The statement gives n, m and the edges. Read it in, pick an algorithm. Nothing to model.
14.2.2 2. Grid
Cells are vertices, adjacent free cells are edges. Never build the adjacency list, use the dx/dy loop
(Part 2).
Watch for the variations: walls, teleporters (extra edges), different costs per cell (Dijkstra), moves
that change direction (state expansion, see below).
14.2.3 3. State graph
The vertices are configurations, the edges are legal moves. The classic examples:
"minimum button presses to turn number x into y"
vertex = current number
edges = the operations, each costing 1
-> BFS
"minimum moves of a sliding puzzle"
vertex = the whole board configuration
edges = sliding one tile
-> BFS, with a map<string,int> for distances
"can you measure exactly 4 litres with jugs of 3 and 5"
vertex = (amount in jug A, amount in jug B)
edges = fill, empty, pour
-> BFS
The test for this family: the problem asks for theminimum number of operations, and each operation
transforms one situation into another. That is BFS on states, always.
Before coding, count the states. Jugs of size 100 give 101 * 101 = 10201 states, which is nothing. A
board of 20 items with a permutation state gives 20 factorial, which is impossible. The state count is
your feasibility check.
14.2.4 4. State expansion
The answer depends on the vertex and something else. Put the something else into the vertex.
"shortest path, you may use at most k free edges"
state = (vertex, number of free edges used)
size = n * (k + 1)

--- Page Break ---

How to Think About Graph Problems 91
"shortest path, but you must arrive with an even number of steps"
state = (vertex, parity)
size = 2n
"shortest path on a grid where turning costs 1 and going straight is free"
state = (cell, current direction)
size = 4 * R * C, and it is a 0-1 BFS
"cheapest route with at most one refuel"
state = (city, fuel remaining)
The algorithm does not change. Dijkstra on the expanded graph is still Dijkstra. Only your d array
grows an extra dimension: d[v][k] instead of d[v].
14.2.5 5. Node splitting
A constraint on a vertex (a capacity , a cost to pass through, a limit on visits) cannot be expressed with
edge weights. Split the vertex into v_in and v_out, joined by an edge carrying the vertex’s property .
All original incoming edges go to v_in, all outgoing edges leave v_out.
14.2.6 6. Super source and super sink
“You may start from any of these k vertices” becomes: add vertex 0, join it to each of the k with weight
0, run a single search from 0. Same for “you may finish at any of these”.
The MST version of this trick, where a vertex represents “build your own power plant”, was in Part 10.
14.2.7 7. Reverse the graph
“What is the distance from every vertex to vertex t” is not a single-source problem, until you reverse
every edge and run a single search from t. This turns an n-times problem into a once problem. Reach
for it whenever the target is fixed and the source varies.
14.2.8 8. Complement graph
Sometimes the graph you need is the complement of the given one, and the given one is dense while
the complement is sparse. There is a standard technique using a set of unvisited vertices during BFS,
which keeps the total work at O(n + m). Know it exists.
14.2.9 9. Dependencies become a DAG
“A must come before B”, “you must learn X before Y”, “the letters are in some unknown alphabet
order”. Build an edge for each constraint and topologically sort. If the sort fails, the constraints
contradict each other, and reporting that is usually the point of the problem. Codeforces 510C is the
model example.
14.2.10 10. Equivalence becomes DSU
“These two are interchangeable”, “swap positions i and j freely”, “these accounts belong to the same
person”. Union them all, then work per group. The moment a problem says “and this relation is
transitive”, it is DSU.

--- Page Break ---

How to Think About Graph Problems 92
14.2.11 11. Two options per item becomes 2-colouring
“Each person joins one of two teams and enemies must be separated” is bipartiteness. If the constraints
get more complicated (“if A is in team 1 then B must be in team 2”), you are looking at 2-SAT, which
is implication edges plus SCC. That is beyond this course, but Part 13 gave you its machinery .
14.2.12 12. i -> a[i] is a functional graph
An array of pointers, a permutation, “the winner of match i plays match a[i]”. Every vertex has
outdegree 1, so the structure is always a set of cycles with trees hanging off them. Questions about
“eventually you come back” are about the cycle.
14.3 The decision guide
Is the answer "minimum number of moves" and every move costs the same?
yes -> BFS (expand the state if the answer needs more than a position)
Are there weights?
0/1 -> deque BFS
non-negative -> Dijkstra
negative -> Bellman-Ford
all pairs, n small -> Floyd
Is it "who must come before whom", or "is this possible without contradiction"?
-> topological sort on a DAG, and a failed sort means a cycle
Is it "are these two in the same group", especially with edges arriving over time?
-> DSU
Is it "connect everything as cheaply as possible"?
-> MST
Is it "which single edge or vertex breaks the graph"?
-> bridges and articulation points
Is it a directed graph where cycles are getting in the way?
-> SCC, then work on the condensation DAG
Is it a tree, and the question is about paths or subtrees?
-> root it, subtree DP, LCA
14.4 Pattern to problem map
Pattern Signature in the statement Algorithm
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Reachability "can you get from a to b" DFS or BFS
Components "how many groups / regions" DFS or DSU

--- Page Break ---

How to Think About Graph Problems 93
Shortest unweighted "minimum number of moves" BFS
Nearest of many sources "distance to the closest X" multi-source BFS
Shortest weighted "minimum total cost" Dijkstra
Negative costs "you may gain money" Bellman-Ford
All pairs "q queries about any two" Floyd, n small
Ordering "must be done before" topological sort
Feasibility of order "is it possible" topological sort fails
Cheapest connection "connect all cities" MST
Dynamic connectivity "after each new road" DSU
Critical edges "which road, if closed" bridges
Critical vertices "which city, if destroyed" articulation points
Directed connectivity "everyone can reach everyone" SCC
Tree paths "distance between two nodes" LCA
Tree subtrees "for each subtree" subtree DP
State search "minimum operations" BFS on states
Extra dimension "at most k times you may" state expansion
14.5 Three worked examples
14.5.1 Example A
“There are n cities and m one-way roads. You start in city 1. Find the minimum number of
roads you must reverse so that city n becomes reachable.”
• Vertices: cities. Edges: roads.
• Directed. Weighted? Not stated, but reversing costs something.
• The move: use a road forwards for free, or backwards at a cost of 1.
• So build two edges per road: u -> v with weight 0, and v -> u with weight 1.
• Weights are 0 and 1, so this is 0-1 BFS. O(n + m).
Question 2 (“what does one edge mean”) did all the work.
14.5.2 Example B
“A grid with walls. You may break at most k walls. Find the minimum number of steps
from the top left to the bottom right.”
• The vertex is not a cell. Two visits to the same cell are different if you have broken different
numbers of walls.
• State: (row, column, walls broken so far). Size R * C * (k + 1).
• Every move costs 1, so BFS on states.
• dist[R][C][k+1], and moving into a wall increases the third coordinate.
Question 9 did all the work.
14.5.3 Example C
“n people, and m statements of the form ‘i and j are the same species’. Then q queries
asking whether two people are the same species.”

--- Page Break ---

How to Think About Graph Problems 94
• No distances, no ordering. Just “same group”, and the relation is transitive.
• DSU. Union each statement, answer each query with find(a) == find(b).
• If the statements could also say “i and j are different species, and there are exactly two species”, it
becomes bipartite checking, or DSU with parity .
Question 6 did all the work.
14.6 When you are stuck
In order:
1. Draw a small case, 5 or 6 vertices, and solve it by hand. Then ask what you did.
2. Say the vertex set out loud. “A vertex is a cell together with the direction I am facing.” If you
cannot finish that sentence, that is the blocker.
3. Count the states. If it is 1012, your model is wrong, not your code.
4. Look at the constraints again. n <= 500 with q queries screams Floyd. n <= 20 screams
bitmask. m <= 2*105 screams O(m log n).
5. Check whether a transformation makes it standard: reverse, super source, split, condense.
6. Ask what makes it non-standard, and put that thing into the state.
14.7 Habits of strong contestants
• They write the vertex definition as a comment before writing code.
• They compute the state count and compare it with the time limit before implementing.
• They test on: a disconnected graph, a single vertex, a self loop if allowed, and the largest n.
• They use long long for any sum of weights, by default.
• They keep a personal template file with DSU, Dijkstra, BFS and the DFS skeletons, so implementa-
tion time goes to the modelling.
• They read the constraints before the statement.
14.8 Check yourself
1. A problem asks for the minimum number of operations to turn one string into another using a
fixed set of moves. What are the vertices, and which algorithm?
2. You may use a “teleport” at most twice on a shortest path. How does the state change?
3. The problem asks for the distance from every city to the capital. Why reverse the edges?
4. A statement says “each of the m constraints says task a must precede task b, report any valid
schedule or say it is impossible”. Name the algorithm and the failure test.
5. Costs are 0 and 1. Why not just use Dijkstra? What do you gain from the deque?
6. When does “same group and transitive” not mean DSU?
7. You modelled a problem and the state count is 10 11. What do you do next?

--- Page Break ---

metadata.section_title: Part 14 - How to Think About Graph Problems

section_based.text:
Part 15
Practice Problem Sets
Graded Codeforces problems, with hints and no solutions
15.1 How to use this set
1. Answer the “think about” line before writing code. That line is the exercise. The typing is not.
2. Time yourself: 25 minutes for a Level 1 or 2 problem, 45 for Level 4. If you are stuck past that,
read one hint, not an editorial.
3. After solving, name the pattern out loud. “That was multi-source BFS.” Naming is what makes
the next one faster.
4. Always test: a disconnected graph, n = 1, the maximum n, and self loops if the statement allows
them.
5. Redo, do not collect. Twenty problems solved twice beats forty solved once.
Difficulty ratings below are approximate. Use them as a rough ladder, not as gospel.
15.2 A note on where to practise
Codeforces is where you compete, so its problems are the ones listed here. But for the very first
exposure to each algorithm, the CSES Graph section is better designed: one clean problem per
technique, no story, no twist. If you are starting from zero, do the CSES list in parallel. It is at
https://cses.fi/problemset/ under “Graph Algorithms”, and the first ten problems there map almost
exactly onto Parts 3 to 11 of this course.
15.3 Level 1: first graph problems
Goal: get DFS, BFS and DSU into your fingers. Nothing here needs a clever idea.
• Books Exchange (easy version), 1249B1. ~1100. https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/
1249/B1 Pattern: functional graph, cycle lengths. Think: i -> p[i] gives every vertex outdegree
1. What shape must the graph be?
• Ice Skating, 217A. ~1200. https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/217/A Pattern:
components. Think: what exactly is an edge here, and what does the answer c - 1 mean?
• Party, 115A. ~1100. https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/115/A Pattern: depth in a
forest. Think: can you compute each chain length by walking up, and is that fast enough?
• DZY Loves Chemistry, 445B. ~1300. https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/445/B
Pattern: components with DSU. Think: what is the contribution of a component of size k?
95

--- Page Break ---

Practice Problem Sets 96
• Fox And Two Dots, 510B. ~1500 but conceptually easy . https://codeforces.com/problemset/pr
oblem/510/B Pattern: cycle detection on a grid. Think: which neighbour must you skip, and why
is that not enough with multi-edges (here, is it a problem)?

Vocabulary, and how a graph differs from a tree
1.1 Why graphs exist
A tree can express hierarchy: one parent, many children, no way back up except the way you came.
That is a strong restriction, and most real relationships break it.
• Cities joined by roads. A city has no parent. You can drive in a circle.
• Friendships. If A is a friend of B then B is a friend of A. Not a hierarchy .
• Course prerequisites. Many courses depend on many others, and the dependency has a direction.
• Web pages linking to each other. Circular links are normal.
• States of a puzzle, where a move takes you from one state to another.
A graph is the most general “things and connections between them” structure. Trees, linked lists, grids
and hierarchies are all special cases of it. That generality is exactly why graphs are the single largest
topic in competitive programming.

1.2 Definition
A graph is a pair G = (V, E):
• V is a set of vertices, also called nodes. We number them 1 to n.
• E is a set of edges, each edge joining two vertices.
That is the whole definition. There is no root, no parent, no order among the neighbours of a vertex,
and no guarantee that everything is connected.

The four practical consequences, and you should write them on the first page of your notebook:
1. Always keep a visited array. Without it, DFS on a cyclic graph never terminates.
2. Always loop over all vertices when you want to cover the whole graph, because one DFS only
covers one component.
3. Complexity is O(n + m), not O(n). You touch every vertex once and every adjacency entry once,
and every undirected edge appears in two lists.
4. Recursion can go n deep. With n = 2 * 105 and heavy stack frames, plain DFS can crash. Keep
the frame small, or write it iteratively .
A tree is not a different data structure from a graph. A tree is a connected undirected graph with
no cycles, equivalently a connected graph with exactly n - 1 edges. Part 12 revisits the whole trees
course in graph language, and everything you learned there still works.
1.7 Families of graphs worth naming

In an undirected graph, every non-tree edge joins a vertex to one of its own ancestors. Such an edge

descendant), and cross (to an already-finished vertex elsewhere). Only back edges indicate a cycle.

Same as the level order traversal from the trees course: finish everything at distance 1, then everything
at distance 2, and so on. The queue is the same queue.
The difference from trees is again the visited check, and the payoff is bigger here, because BFS on a

here, because BFS on a
graph answers a question DFS cannot:

every other vertex.
That sentence is the reason BFS matters. Memorise it with its condition: unweighted. The moment
edges have different weights, BFS is wrong and you need Part 11.
4.2 Why the layers are shortest distances
BFS processes vertices in non-decreasing order of distance. The argument is short enough to keep in
your head:
• Layer 0 is {s}, at distance 0, obviously correct.
• Suppose every vertex at distance k has been placed in the queue and nothing further has been.
When we pop those vertices and push their unvisited neighbours, any such neighbour must be at
distance exactly k + 1: it cannot be closer, or it would already have been found in an earlier layer,
and it is reachable in k + 1 steps by construction.
So the first time BFS reaches a vertex, it reaches it optimally. That is why we set dist and mark
visited at push time, not at pop time.

A graph is bipartite if you can split the vertices into two groups so that every edge goes between
the groups, and no edge stays inside a group.
