A graph is bipartite if and only if it contains no cycle of odd length.
The forward direction is easy to see. Walk along a cycle: the colour alternates at every step, so to
come back to the starting vertex with the starting colour, the number of steps must be even.

Part 9
Disjoint Set Union
The competitive programmer’s favourite data structure
9.1 The problem it solves
You have n items, initially all separate. Two operations arrive in any order, many times:
union(a, b) put a and b into the same group
find(a) which group is a in
and the real question is usually find(a) == find(b), meaning “are a and b in the same group”.
DFS answers connectivity once, in O(n + m). It cannot handle edges arriving over time, because
every new edge would need a fresh traversal. DSU handles both operations in essentially constant
time, which is why it appears in an enormous fraction of contest problems.
Other names for it: Union-Find, disjoint set forest.
9.2 The idea
Every group is a tree, and the root of that tree is the group’s name. find(x) walks up to

Correct, and potentially O(n) per operation. Union in a bad order builds a chain:
union(1,2), union(2,3), union(3,4), ... produces
1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> ... -> n
and find(1) walks the entire chain.
Two independent improvements fix this. Use both.
9.4 Improvement 1: path compression
While walking up in find, point every visited node straight at the root. The next find on any of them
is then one step.
int find(int x) {
if (parent[x] == x) return x;
return parent[x] = find(parent[x]); // compress on the way back up
}
That single line,parent[x] = find(parent[x]), does the whole job. It is a postorder assignment:
recurse to the root first, then rewrite the pointer.

9.5 Improvement 2: union by size
Always hang the smaller tree under the larger one. Then no tree ever gets deep, because a tree only
gains depth when it is merged into something

9.6 Complexity
With both improvements, m operations on n elements cost O(m alpha(n)), where alpha is the inverse
Ackermann function. For any n that fits in the universe, alpha(n) <= 4. So treat it as constant time
and write O(m) or O(n + m) in your analysis.
With only path compression, or only union by size, it is O(log n) per operation, which is also fine in
practice. With neither, it is O(n) per operation and it will fail.

10.1 The problem
Given a connected undirected weighted graph, choose a subset of edges that

. keeps everything connected, and

Such a subset is always a tree on all n vertices: it has exactly n - 1 edges and no cycles. If it had a
cycle you could delete an edge of that cycle and stay connected while paying less. Hence the name
minimum spanning tree, MST.
Typical phrasing in problems: connect all cities with roads at minimum cost; lay cable so every house
has power; make the network connected as cheaply as possible.
If the graph is disconnected there is no spanning tree. Then the answer is usually a minimum
spanning forest, one tree per component, and the problem will say so or will guarantee connectivity .

10.3 The one idea behind both algorithms
The cut property. Split the vertices into any two non-empty groups. Look at all edges crossing
between the groups. The cheapest one of those can always be part of some MST.

your tree uses a more expensive crossing edge, swap it for the cheapest one. You stay connected and

the only real difference between them.

11.5.3 Detecting a negative cycle
If any edge can still be relaxed after n - 1 rounds, some path is getting shorter forever, which means
a negative cycle is reachable from the source. To find which vertices are affected, run one more
round and mark every vertex you improve, then propagate that mark along all outgoing edges with a
BFS or DFS.
Time O(n m). Space O(n + m).
That complexity is why Bellman-Ford is the last resort. With n and m both 105 it is 1010 operations and
hopeless. It is used when n is small, or when negative weights genuinely appear (currency arbitrage,

A bridge is an edge whose removal increases the number of connected components. Also called a cut

The tree edge u - v (with v a child of u) is a bridge if and only if low[v] > tin[u].

13.6 Common mistakes
• Using low[v] instead of tin[v] on a back edge. The classic.
• Using > instead of >= for articulation points, or the reverse for bridges.
• Forgetting the special rule for the root.
• Skipping the parent by vertex when multi-edges exist. Skip by edge index.
• Forgetting to run the outer loop over all vertices on a disconnected graph.
• Building the reversed graph incorrectly in Kosaraju, most often by reversing only some edges.
• Assuming the condensation might have a cycle. It cannot.
• Recursion depth. These are all DFS, so a 2 * 105 chain is a real risk.

14.2.7 7. Reverse the graph
“What is the distance from every vertex to vertex t” is not a single-source problem, until you reverse
every edge and run a single search from t. This turns an n-times problem into a once problem. Reach

Sometimes the graph you need is the complement of the given one, and the given one is dense while
the complement is sparse. There is a standard technique using a set of unvisited vertices during BFS,
which keeps the total work at O(n + m). Know it exists.

contradict each other, and reporting that is usually the point of the problem. Codeforces 510C is the
model example.

14.6 When you are stuck
In order:
1. Draw a small case, 5 or 6 vertices, and solve it by hand. Then ask what you did.
2. Say the vertex set out loud. “A vertex is a cell together with the direction I am facing.” If you
cannot finish that sentence, that is the blocker.
3. Count the states. If it is 1012, your model is wrong, not your code.
4. Look at the constraints again. n <= 500 with q queries screams Floyd. n <= 20 screams
bitmask. m <= 2*105 screams O(m log n).
5. Check whether a transformation makes it standard: reverse, super source, split, condense.
6. Ask what makes it non-standard, and put that thing into the state.
